## 1-PRIOR. US-Iran Military Actions — JULY 31-AUGUST 1 (DAY 156): THE UNITED STATES PICKS ITS INSTRUMENT — A MULTI-DAY BOMBING CAMPAIGN AGAINST IRAN'S ENERGY AND CIVIL INFRASTRUCTURE, REPORTED AS AIMED AT FORCING SURRENDER AND ABLE TO BEGIN AS SOON AS THE WEEKEND. THE TARGET CLASSES ARE POWER PLANTS, REFINERIES, TEHRAN'S ELECTRICITY GRID AND DUAL-USE BRIDGES — AND NO GROUND ELEMENT AND NO KHARG OPERATION APPEARS IN ANY VERSION OF THE REPORTING. THE ORDER'S STATUS IS ITSELF CONTESTED: THE WSJ SAYS ORDERED, CBS SAYS NO FINAL AUTHORISATION, CNN SAYS IT COULD BE CALLED OFF, AND AN ISRAELI OFFICIAL SAYS ISRAEL IS 'UNAWARE OF A DECISION.' IRAN ANSWERS BY ONE-WAY DRONE ACROSS THREE COUNTRIES — SHEIKH ISA, AHMAD AL-JABER, ALI AL-SALEM AND AL AZRAQ. US WOUNDED RISE 32 TO 685. CENTCOM CONFIRMS IT IS INVESTIGATING THE QESHM DEATHS OF A TWO-YEAR-OLD AND THE CHILD'S PARENTS. TEHRAN DENIES DAMIETTA AND CAIRO REJECTS THE ATTRIBUTION REPORTED ON ITS BEHALF. RIYADH CONVENES 43 NATIONS FOR A MARITIME COALITION WASHINGTON COULD NOT RAISE. BAGHDAD CONTRADICTS THE PRESIDENT. BRENT CLOSES JULY UP ~24%; DIESEL SETS ANOTHER WAR HIGH. GROUND RUNG: EVERY EXECUTION INDICATOR AT ZERO FOR A 156TH DAY.

**A campaign is reported, and its declared purpose is capitulation.** The *Wall Street Journal*, citing US officials, reported on July 31 that President Trump has ordered another wave of strikes against Iran with the aim of forcing the Islamic Republic's surrender, that the bombing is expected to last several days, and that it could start as soon as this weekend. *CBS News*, citing multiple US sources, reported that the United States and Israel are preparing to bombard energy-related targets in Iran. *Axios* reported that Trump was considering strikes on Iranian energy targets within days. *CNN*, citing two US officials, reported fresh strikes as soon as this weekend, while noting that the precise scope and potential targets were not clear and that both officials cautioned the strikes could be called off. The convergence across four outlets on the same day, on the same target concept, is the substance; the disagreement is about whether it has been authorised.

**What is being targeted.** CBS named the likely target set as **power plants and refineries**, with **electricity infrastructure across Tehran** under high-level discussion but no decision as of Friday, and **bridges used for dual military-civilian purposes** also under consideration. Strikes were described as possible throughout the weekend, with an end point not locked in and discussion of concluding before financial markets opened Monday — a detail that locates the campaign's design constraints as much in the oil and equity markets as in the target folder. The plan was raised at Trump's Friday cabinet meeting at Camp David, where he said: "We'll be hitting them very hard. At some point, they're going to say, 'We just can't take it anymore.'" One source said White House aides focused on politics "were strongly opposed."

**The dispute over whether it has been ordered.** The WSJ framing is that Trump has ordered it. CBS reported that the president has **not** yet given final authorisation and that the plan remains pending his decision. An Israeli official said: "Israel is unaware of a decision to restart full military operations, nor has been requested of Israel to join any military actions against Iran" — stated against multiple US sources telling CBS that Israel had been notified of the potential strikes and was coordinating with the American military. No execute order, air tasking order, War Powers notification or on-record confirmation or denial by Trump, Secretary Hegseth, the Pentagon or CENTCOM has been published. The dispute is logged in `open-questions.json` as `iran-energy-strike-campaign-order-status-july-2026`; this briefing records the reporting and scores on execution.

**The absence that matters most.** In none of the four reports does a ground element appear. No landing force, no embarkation, no Marine Expeditionary Unit tasking, no airborne insertion, no raid, and no Kharg Island operation is named. This is not merely an absence of evidence for a ground phase; it is evidence about instrument selection. The Kharg-seizure option reported since March 2026 — two MEUs, roughly 1,000-2,000 soldiers of the 82nd Airborne, an amphibious landing against a shoreline Iran has mined with anti-personnel and anti-armour munitions — existed to supply precisely the coercive leverage this air campaign is now reported to be seeking: forcing Iran to accept American terms on the Strait. When a state facing one objective holds two instruments and the reported choice is the air instrument, that bears on the ground rung even though nothing on the ground rung moved. It does not foreclose a ground phase — a campaign that fails to force terms is exactly the circumstance in which the Kharg option returns, and the coastal-suppression strikes of July 29-30 would shape the approach for one.

**Trump's public posture: losing faith, not closing the door.** Asked whether a deal remained possible, Trump said: "Yes, you can. I mean, I'm losing faith in them because they do lie," adding that "Iran is doing very poorly... they're doing very, very poorly." The formulation preserves both tracks — a campaign designed to compel and a negotiation the compulsion is meant to serve.

**Iran answers by drone, across the Gulf, against bases.** Iran's army said its one-way attack drones struck US assets at **Sheikh Isa Air Base** in southern Bahrain, which Iran's military called "one of the most important US military installations in the Gulf region," targeting power generators, navigation systems, and administrative and support buildings. Iran said the operation was carried out "in retaliation for the killing of an Iranian Air Force Su-24 pilot at the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran in February." Iran's army separately said it targeted aircraft shelters, satellite communication systems and equipment storage facilities used by the US military at Kuwait's **Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base**; the IRGC claimed attacks on US assets at **Ali al-Salem Air Base** in Kuwait and **Al Azraq Air Base** in Jordan. Iran claimed its recent attacks had inflicted "significant damage" on military equipment and facilities and "serious damage to the base's combat and logistical support capabilities."

**And is met with silence.** There was no immediate comment from Bahraini or US authorities on any of the claims, and no casualties were reported. This repeats the evidentiary structure of July 30, when CENTCOM categorically denied the IRGC's claim to have destroyed three F-35s at Al Azraq while saying nothing about the claimed US personnel casualties. Absence of denial is not corroboration and absence of imagery is not refutation; damage on host-nation soil is not independently observable, and the Gulf host governments have consistently declined to detail what Iranian attacks cost them.

**The human ledger.** The running US casualty tally reached **685 wounded** and **18 killed in action** on July 31, up 32 wounded from the 653 reported at 9:06 PM GMT on July 30, which had itself been 11 higher than Tuesday's figure — the largest single-cycle increase since the Pentagon's unexplained July reclassification, and spanning Iran's ballistic attack on Jordan, the July 29-30 US "heavy wave" and Iran's drone retaliation against Gulf air bases. On the Iranian side, US Central Command acknowledged that it is **investigating** reports that an Iranian two-year-old and the child's parents were killed in the July 30 strike on Qeshm Island; a CENTCOM spokesman said: "The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike Iranian forces." Cumulative independent counts remain contested — HRANA has documented roughly 3,636 Iranian casualties and Iran's Foundation of Martyrs confirms 3,468, figures combining military and civilian dead.

**Damietta moves away from Tehran without being resolved.** Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi denied Iranian involvement in the July 29 drone attack on Egypt's Damietta port, writing that "Egypt is an important friend and partner in the region," that Cairo's security is of utmost importance to Tehran, and warning: "We must all be vigilant against Israeli plots and false-flag operations designed to undermine regional peace." Egypt's Minister of State for Information **Diaa Rashwan** publicly dismissed a *Wall Street Journal* report claiming the Egyptian government believed Iran was responsible. Egyptian authorities said no group had claimed responsibility, that drone wreckage had been recovered for forensic analysis, and that the investigation was ongoing; Prime Minister **Mostafa Madbouly** said security agencies were examining the debris to determine its origin. Cairo condemned the strike and warned against further escalation while naming no one. President Trump's July 30 attribution to Iran, made without published evidence, stands unretracted and uncorroborated. Every actor's stated position is the one its own incentives predict.

**Riyadh raises the coalition Washington could not.** Saudi Arabia's Defence Ministry convened **military representatives of 43 countries in Riyadh on Thursday, July 30**, to stand up a multinational **maritime defence coalition** aimed at enhancing maritime security, protecting international maritime corridors and countering threats to maritime navigation and global trade, with a geographic focus on the **Bab al-Mandeb strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden** and proposed activities comprising joint maritime operations, intelligence sharing, training and joint exercises. The headquarters would sit in the kingdom. Thirteen states publicly backed the initiative — **Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Pakistan, Turkey, Egypt, Jordan, Yemen, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Sudan, Djibouti and Somalia**. The contrast with the American effort is the cycle's clearest measure of who can raise a naval coalition and where: POLITICO reported two days earlier that Hegseth is urging Britain and France to help lead the Hormuz escort coalition and that European allies are refusing until they see an enduring ceasefire, with no movement expected soon. The driver is structural — the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of the kingdom on July 20, and **Yanbu**, outlet of the East-West Pipeline, handled roughly **92% of Saudi seaborne crude exports in June 2026** after Hormuz closed, with every cargo loading there obliged to transit the Bab al-Mandeb.

**Baghdad contradicts the President.** On July 31 the Iraqi government stated it had **no prior knowledge** of the July 28 US-Saudi strikes on Popular Mobilisation Forces positions, directly contradicting President Trump's statement that the operation had been coordinated with Baghdad. Iraq's National Security Council, chaired by Prime Minister **Ali al-Zaidi**, had already called the attacks on PMF bases across seven provinces "a flagrant violation of Iraq's sovereignty and the sanctity of its lands" and "an aggression" contrary to international law and the UN Charter. Baghdad suspended al-Zaidi's planned visit to Saudi Arabia. The prime minister has separately committed to disarming the armed groups and bringing weapons under state control by **September 30, 2026** — the date on which US forces are scheduled to withdraw from Iraq. The consultation dispute is logged as `iraq-prior-knowledge-us-saudi-strikes-july-2026`.

**Markets and the Strait.** Brent settled at **$90.24**, up $3.36 or **3.87%** on the day, closing July with a gain of roughly **24%** — its strongest monthly increase since March — with analysts projecting $101.25 by quarter-end; the straits.live board showed the same price with a 24-hour change of +2.36% at 20:52 UTC against a pre-crisis baseline of about $72 (+25.3%). That a reported campaign to destroy Iran's refining capacity produced a 3.87% move rather than a supply-panic repricing is itself the market's assessment. AAA's national average reached **$4.1060** for regular (from $4.0980; $3.8470 a month ago, $3.1470 a year ago) and **$5.3530** for diesel (from $5.3390; $4.8530 a month ago, $3.7410 a year ago) — another war high, within about 46 cents of the June 2022 record of $5.816, with diesel up on every day of the past week irrespective of crude's direction. On the water, S&P Global recorded **28 Hormuz transits on July 29**, the highest since July 14, driven by **resumed LNG tanker traffic after a two-week gap**, with Iran-linked vessels at 60% of movements from a 68% second-half-of-July average; Bab el-Mandeb crossings rose to 39 and VLCCs increasingly gathered at Egypt's **Sidi Kerir** terminal. The straits.live board reverted to its prior framing — latest recorded volume of **10 transits** against an **88/day** pre-crisis baseline, or **11% of normal throughput**, **1,364 vessels stranded** (up 109 on 29 hours earlier), **85 AIS-dark tankers** against a 42.4 seven-day baseline, war-risk insurance at **8.0x peacetime**, and prediction markets pricing a 1% probability of normalised traffic by August 1 — which supports the previous cycle's assessment that the July 30 readings reflected a zone-definition change rather than a reopening. Iran's Fars agency said the Revolutionary Guards **stopped two tankers** while **four others altered course**; the CENTCOM interdiction tally holds at 18 vessels stopped, 2 disabled and 2 boarded with 20+ warships committed.

**Ground-invasion indicators — zero for a 156th day, and the most informative cycle since March.** Nothing on the ground rung moved, and the reason this cycle matters is that the alternative to it was described in full. (1) The reported plan for forcing Iranian capitulation is an **air** plan, in target-class detail, across four outlets, with **no ground component**. (2) **Kharg Island was not named** as a target, was not struck in the July 29-30 wave, and has never been seized; Iran's fortification of the island, including mines on the shoreline where a landing would stage, stands as last reported. (3) The **amphibious picture is unchanged for a tenth day**: USS *Boxer* (LHD-4) remains in the **Arabian Sea** — outside the Gulf — with USS *Comstock* (LSD-45), USS *Portland* (LPD-27) and the 11th MEU, still the **sole deployed ARG fleet-wide** per the July 27 USNI tracker, the most recent edition; no relief ARG has been announced and USS *Tripoli* is home in Sasebo. (4) **Troop strength is unchanged** at roughly 50,000 in the Middle East, including approximately 2,000 soldiers of the 82nd Airborne with divisional headquarters, in theatre since late March and never committed to Iranian soil. (5) **Iran's own escalation was on the air rung** — one-way drones against Gulf air bases, not a ground action. (6) The **draft rung remains down**: the Selective Service's automatic-registration rule, withdrawn July 23, has not been re-proposed and no explanation has been given; the December 19, 2026 statutory deadline is unchanged; automatic registration is not a draft and none has been called or planned. Every execution indicator stood at zero for a 156th consecutive day: no US troops in Iran, no landing, no Kharg seizure, no new ARG or MEU order, no draft. **The predicted US GROUND seizure of Hormuz or Kharg remains DISCONFIRMED.**

**Other theatres (July 30-31, 2026).** *Russia-Ukraine:* a projectile assessed by experts as a Russian **Kh-101 cruise missile** crossed into Polish airspace during Russia's overnight barrage and detonated in a field near **Tarnawa-Kolonia**, outside **Lublin**, leaving a ten-metre crater; NATO's military headquarters said the alliance activated a wide range of air defences, fighters were scrambled, and NATO said it would "defend territory," with Warsaw blaming Moscow and no Polish casualties reported. The barrage itself — more than 70 missiles and about 280 drones against Kyiv and Lviv — killed at least eight including three children, with later counts of nine and ten. On July 31 Ukrainian long-range strikes hit oil refineries and Wildberries logistics facilities in Volgograd, Tatarstan and Krasnodar, after Zelensky's July 30 pledge to intensify strikes on Russian territory. Ukraine's General Staff recorded 226 combat clashes by 22:00 on July 30, heaviest at Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk; The Economist put Russia's thirty-day territorial gain at zero square miles and DeepState the four-week net at ten, against thirty-one in the prior period. *Venezuela:* US-backed transition talks open August 1 with National Assembly chief **Jorge Rodríguez** — brother of interim president Delcy Rodríguez — heading the government delegation and **Dinorah Figuera** the opposition, and **María Corina Machado** declining to participate while not opposing the talks; Maduro and Cilia Flores remain set for trial before Judge Alvin Hellerstein on June 1, 2027. *Lebanon:* the IDF said on July 31 it had demolished a multi-level Hezbollah tunnel complex beneath the **Beaufort Ridge** with **700 tonnes of explosives**, describing it as the Bader Unit's central command post, built over two decades, six kilometres from Metula and funded by Iran; the next round of US-brokered Israel-Lebanon talks is scheduled for **Rome, August 4-6**. *China:* Beijing's position is unchanged — the Foreign Ministry urges both sides to settle disputes through negotiations, carry out the MoU and avoid resorting to force — while China's July crude imports are poised to rebound from a decade low; the Reuters MANPADS report remains denied by both Beijing and Islamabad and unverified; the USTR's 12.5% Section 301 forced-labour tariff, effective July 24, remains the operative new trade measure. *Korean Peninsula:* no new provocation; Kim Jong Un's naval build-out continues, with the destroyer *Kang Kon* to be commissioned by September and a 10,000-tonne guided-missile cruiser in development.

## 1-PRIOR. US-Iran Military Actions — JULY 30-31 (DAY 155): THE UNITED STATES GOES BACK TO BOMBING IRAN ITSELF — A 'HEAVY WAVE' AGAINST 'DOZENS' OF IRGC TARGETS OVER ROUGHLY TWO HOURS, THE FIRST STRIKE ON IRANIAN SOIL SINCE JULY 24 AND 'ABOUT TWICE THE SIZE OF THE PREVIOUS' BOMBARDMENT. THE TARGET SET IS THE GULF LITTORAL — 'COASTAL SURVEILLANCE AND DEFENSE SITES' AND 'MARITIME CAPABILITIES' AT BANDAR ABBAS, QESHM, KISH, ABU MUSA, BUSHEHR, KAZERUN, FARASHBAND, ABADAN AND AHVAZ — BUT NOT KHARG. IRNA REPORTS THREE KILLED ON QESHM, IDENTIFIED AS A COUPLE AND THEIR TWO-YEAR-OLD CHILD. THE IRGC VOWS 'THE AGGRESSOR WILL BE PUNISHED TODAY,' THREATENS STATES AIDING THE US, CLAIMS 'FULL CONTROL' OF THE STRAIT, AND ASSERTS IT DESTROYED THREE F-35s AT AL AZRAQ — CENTCOM DENIES THE AIRCRAFT AND IS SILENT ON THE CLAIMED CASUALTIES. THE WAR WIDENS TWICE: AN IRANIAN STRIKE KILLS A WORKER AT A CHINESE COMPANY'S BUILDING IN KUWAIT, AND AN UNCLAIMED DRONE HITS TWO LNG VESSELS AT EGYPT'S DAMIETTA — THE FIRST ATTACK ON EGYPTIAN SOIL OF THE WAR, AND ON AN IMPORT TERMINAL. SAUDI ARABIA FLIES STRIKES ONE DAY AND ARGUES FOR DE-ESCALATION IN THE OVAL OFFICE THE NEXT. BAGHDAD SUMMONS BOTH AMBASSADORS. BRENT EASES BELOW $90; DIESEL SETS ANOTHER WAR HIGH. GROUND RUNG: THE FIRST AMBIGUOUS SHAPING SIGNAL OF THE WAR, WITH EVERY EXECUTION INDICATOR STILL AT ZERO.

**The strikes on Iranian territory resume, at roughly double scale.** US Central Command announced overnight into July 30 that it had "successfully completed a heavy wave of strikes against Iran," saying its forces "struck dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran, including military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities." The operation ran approximately two hours. A US official told *The Jerusalem Post* the bombardment was "about twice the size of the previous" one, and described the effect as "wide, extensive, and impactful." The stated predicate was the IRGC's July 28 attempted ballistic attack on US forces, which CENTCOM said was fully intercepted, and Trump's framing afterwards that it was now "our turn." This is the first American munition on Iranian soil since July 24 — a six-day interval in which the United States struck Iran's proxies in Iraq but not Iran.

**Where it landed, and what that geography means.** The reported strike map is the most legible of the war, and it is a coastline. Explosions were reported at Bandar Abbas in Hormozgan; on Qeshm Island (three); on Kish Island (two); at Abu Musa; across three cities of Bushehr province, home to Iran's only civil nuclear power plant; at Kazerun and Farashband in Fars; and at Abadan and Ahvaz in Khuzestan, where seven locations were struck and power went out. Nearly every named site sits on the Persian Gulf littoral or the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz. **Kharg Island was not among the reported targets** — the island that handles roughly 90% of Iran's crude exports and that has been the reported centrepiece of the Pentagon's limited-raid options since March.

**The civilian cost.** Iran's official IRNA news agency said three people were killed and two wounded in a strike on Qeshm. *Al Jazeera* reported the dead as a couple and their two-year-old child, with children aged seven and nine wounded and two further people trapped under rubble; three IRGC personnel were separately reported killed. No independent verification and no consolidated national toll was available at the cycle close, and the competing Iranian figures of the previous cycle — government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani's 350+ government employees killed in the line of duty against Health Minister Zafarghandi's 60 for the southern strikes — remain unreconciled.

**Iran promises same-day retaliation and reasserts the Strait.** The IRGC said early Thursday, via Fars, that "with the help of God Almighty, the aggressor will be punished today." It warned that countries assisting the United States would "receive a harsh response" — a threat aimed at the Gulf hosts and, implicitly, at the naval coalition Washington is trying to raise. And it asserted that it retains "full control" of the Strait of Hormuz, where "a stranger who has come from thousands of kilometres away will not be allowed to interfere." No further Iranian strike had been confirmed when the cycle closed.

**A damage claim, a specific denial, and a conspicuous silence.** The IRGC claimed it had destroyed three F-35 fighter jets at Al Azraq Air Base in Jordan — the installation also identified as Muwaffaq Salti, which it named on July 29 as the target of its July 28 salvo — and that it had killed US personnel there. CENTCOM rejected the aircraft claim categorically, stating that no US aircraft were destroyed or damaged and that all missiles and drones were intercepted. It did not formally address the casualty claim, and *The Washington Times* reported requesting clarification without receiving it. The shape of that response is what makes the question live rather than settled: a specific denial on airframes and a silence on personnel, in a war where the Pentagon has moved four deaths and 207 wounded into an unexplained "Overseas Operations" category. No imagery, and no Jordanian statement on damage, has been published.

**The war reaches Kuwait again — and Egypt for the first time.** Kuwait's Ministry of Defence said an Iranian strike hit a building belonging to a Chinese company in the country's north, killing one worker and causing extensive material damage; spokesman Saud Al-Atwan described it as "Iranian aggression," and the Kuwaiti Armed Forces said they would continue "taking all necessary measures to protect the nation's sovereignty and safeguard its security and stability." The worker's nationality was not stated in the initial official account. Separately, and more consequentially, a drone struck the US-owned, Marshall Islands-flagged floating storage and regasification unit *Energos Winter* at Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta at about 14:20 UTC on July 29, with fire spreading to the Bermuda-flagged LNG carrier *Gaslog Salem*. Both crews were evacuated, the fire was brought under control and no injuries were reported. Egypt's Cabinet confirmed on July 30 that preliminary investigations found a drone caused it, and named no perpetrator; no party claimed responsibility; Trump blamed Iran without presenting evidence. This is the first attack on Egyptian soil since the war began on February 28, and its significance is structural: **Damietta is an import terminal.** For five months the energy war has been fought over an export chokepoint. It has now touched the receiving end of the chain, on the Mediterranean, roughly 2,000 km from the Strait.

**Riyadh fights and sues for peace in consecutive days.** Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman met President Trump and Vice President JD Vance at the White House on July 29, hours after Saudi jets flew joint precision strikes with CENTCOM against militia targets in Iraq. He carried a message from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman: the Kingdom joined the strikes to defend itself after Iranian-backed attacks crossed Riyadh's red line, but the Crown Prince still favours diplomacy over a wider regional war; Netanyahu is pushing for escalation while Saudi Arabia wants de-escalation because it is "a more fruitful path"; and Iran will keep generating leverage through pro-Iranian militias in Iraq and the Houthis in Yemen. He separately lobbied for F-35 sales. The visit had been postponed from the previous week amid an uptick in militia attacks. Reporting on the Trump-Netanyahu session recorded three options canvassed — diplomacy, intensified economic pressure and blockade, or renewed military action — with Netanyahu expressing no preference among them. Oman and Pakistan indicated mediation continues.

**Baghdad hardens and protests in both directions.** Iraq's National Security Council, chaired by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, called the July 28 strikes on PMF sites across seven provinces "a flagrant violation of Iraq's sovereignty and the sanctity of its lands" and "an aggression in contravention of the principles of international law and the United Nations Charter." The presidency called them "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty, targeting its official security institutions." The foreign ministry summoned the US chargé d'affaires and, separately, the Iranian ambassador — a two-sided protest that mirrors the government's structural position between them. Baghdad asserted a right to respond and to self-defence using available means; Iran-aligned factions condemned a "dangerous escalation."

**Markets and the Strait.** Brent surged 7.9% on July 29 on the renewed fighting and then eased back below $90 on July 30 while holding most of that gain: the straits.live tracker showed $89.45, down 1.11% (−$1.00), at 22:59Z, and TradingEconomics recorded Brent falling below $91 and then below $90 intraday. The two-day pattern prices the resumption as a bounded event rather than a supply rupture — the market absorbed both a doubled strike wave and a same-day Iranian retaliation vow without returning to the $100.69 July 23 settle. Pump prices moved the other way again: AAA's national average rose to $4.0980 for regular from $4.0910 and to $5.3390 for diesel from $5.3290, another war high, against $3.140 and $3.740 a year earlier. Diesel has now risen on every day of the past week irrespective of crude direction; distillate tightness, not crude, is setting the print. **The straits.live vessel metrics broke comparability with the prior cycle and are recorded with a flag:** 35 tankers transiting against 10-13, 1,357 vessels anchored or stopped against 339, and 9 dark tankers against 68, with no methodology note published. All three moved by factors of roughly 3-8x in directions that do not reconcile as a single physical event, and no independent source corroborated any of them; this project treats the discontinuity as most likely a change in the counted zone. IMF PortWatch's most recent independent count remains 10 commercial transits on July 23 against an 88-per-day pre-crisis baseline — about 11% of normal throughput. War-risk insurance held at 8.0× pre-crisis, roughly $2.5m for a VLCC; the tracker's Crisis Pressure index read 92 (extreme) and its Escalation Forecast composite 54 (elevated).

**Casualties and force protection.** No new US combat deaths were reported. Total wounded across both categories holds at 642, and the Pentagon's rationale for the new "Overseas Operations" category — that "Operation Epic Fury has concluded" — still comes without any date for the operation's formal end. Separately, US troops in Jordan were warned that their phones may be confiscated in coming days over "operational security concerns," with the CENTCOM commander cautioning that Iran gains real-time visibility of strikes from service members' social-media posts.

**Ground-invasion indicators — zero for a 155th day, and the first ambiguous signal in a week.** This is the first cycle since July 24 to contain a datum pointing toward a ground phase rather than away from one, and it deserves to be stated precisely rather than either inflated or dismissed. CENTCOM's own declared target categories were "coastal surveillance and defense sites" and "maritime capabilities," and the strike map runs along the Gulf littoral from Bandar Abbas through Qeshm, Kish and Abu Musa to Bushehr, Abadan and Ahvaz. Suppressing coastal radar, anti-ship missiles and maritime surveillance along that arc is a **precondition** for the limited Special Operations and conventional raids on Kharg Island and coastal weapons sites that the Pentagon has been reported since late March to hold as options. It is **also** the complete objective, in its own right, of a navy that has been blockading Iranian ports since July 14, escorting convoys through a contested strait, and answering an IRGC that struck three transiting tankers on July 29 and declared third-party mine-clearing vessels "legitimate targets." The two hypotheses generate an identical target list. This briefing records the pattern as an **ambiguous shaping signal and not as evidence of intent**, and continues to score the ground-seizure prediction on execution indicators — all of which remain at zero. Kharg itself was not struck and has never been seized; Iran's fortification of it, including anti-personnel and anti-armour mines on the shoreline where a landing would stage, stands as last reported. No landing occurred anywhere. No new amphibious ready group, Marine Expeditionary Unit or ground formation was ordered, alerted, embarked or repositioned: USS Boxer (LHD-4) remains in the Arabian Sea with USS Comstock (LSD-45), USS Portland (LPD-27) and the 11th MEU, still the sole deployed ARG fleet-wide, with expeditionary sea base USS Miguel Keith (ESB-5) alongside; USS Tripoli (LHA-7) remains home in Sasebo after disembarking 31st MEU elements at Okinawa on July 22, and no relief ARG has been announced nine days on. Carriers Abraham Lincoln and George H.W. Bush remain in the CENTCOM AOR; George Washington is in the South China Sea; Theodore Roosevelt is with RIMPAC 2026. Troop strength holds at approximately 50,000. The Selective Service's proposed automatic-registration rule remains withdrawn since July 23 with no re-proposal and no explanation, the December 19, 2026 statutory deadline unchanged, and no draft called or planned. Britain and France still decline to lead the Hormuz naval coalition absent an enduring ceasefire, and the closest Gulf partner spent the cycle arguing for de-escalation in the Oval Office. **The predicted US GROUND seizure of the Strait of Hormuz or Kharg Island remains DISCONFIRMED for a 155th consecutive day.**

**Other theatres (July 29-30, 2026).** *Russia-Ukraine:* Russia attacked with more than 70 missiles and about 280 drones overnight, killing at least eight by Zelensky's count (later AP-sourced reports gave nine and ten), with Kyiv and the western Lviv region the main focus; Ukraine's air force downed 55 missiles and 265 drones but **only one of nine ballistic missiles**. A Russian cruise missile crossed into Poland and landed in a rural area; NATO confirmed the incursion and scrambled jets; Tusk told an emergency meeting that "all the indications are that it was a Russian Kh-101 ballistic missile, but we want to be 100% certain about the type of missile and who launched it," with no direct threat. *Gulf economics:* the World Bank's 2026 regional growth forecast remains cut from 4.4% to 1.3%, with Oxford Economics projecting some GCC economies entering recession in the second half; around 80 energy facilities have been struck since February; Qatar's Ras Laffan damage stands at 17-20% of capacity with a three-to-five-year restoration and ~$20bn a year in lost revenue, and S&P projects a 5% contraction in Qatari real GDP; the UAE continues to route up to 1.8m bpd via the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline. *Red Sea:* Bab el-Mandeb transits fell to 11 cargo vessels in a day after the Houthi attacks on Saudi shipping, the lowest in months, with the July 20 maritime embargo of Saudi Arabia still in force. *US-China:* the Reuters MANPADS report remains unverified and denied by both Beijing and Islamabad, while an Iranian missile killed a worker in a Chinese company's building in Kuwait; Xi's White House visit is still expected around September 24 and USTR tariff exclusions run to November 10. *Korea:* Kim Jong Un recorded 92 public activities in the first half of 2026, 30 of them military — his highest first-half military count since 2012 — with *Kang Kon* commissioning targeted for September and Sohae satellite preparations continuing. *Latin America:* Venezuela's formal transition talks were set for August 1 with María Corina Machado outside the room; Cuba answered its fourth island-wide grid collapse of the year with its largest private-sector liberalisation of the crisis; Colombia's president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella takes office August 7 pledging to sever ties with Havana.

## 1-PRIOR. US-Iran Military Actions — JULY 29-30 (DAY 154): THE WAR RESUMES ON THREE RUNGS AT ONCE AND THE AMERICAN RETALIATION LANDS IN IRAQ, BY AIR, WITH SAUDI JETS ALONGSIDE. IRAN CLAIMS THE JORDAN STRIKE IT WOULD NOT ACKNOWLEDGE A DAY EARLIER — THE IRGC NAMES MUWAFFAQ SALTI AIR BASE AND A CENTCOM CENTRE, AND JORDAN INTERCEPTS FIVE MISSILES — THEN STRIKES AND STOPS THREE TANKERS IN HORMUZ. TRUMP PROMISES A 'BEATING' WITHOUT NAMING A TARGET, A DATE OR A DOMAIN BEYOND THE AERIAL. CENTCOM AND THE SAUDI ARABIAN ARMED FORCES FLY JOINT PRECISION STRIKES ON MILITIA LOGISTICS IN IRAQ — RIYADH'S FIRST CLAIMED STRIKES INSIDE IRAQ OF THE WAR, UNDER ARTICLE 51, WITH THE PMF REPORTING 20 KILLED AND 32 WOUNDED. IRAN REJECTS OMAN'S HORMUZ PLAN, DEMANDS ONE LANE ENTIRELY IN ITS OWN WATERS PLUS A REPORTED $1M-PER-SHIP FEE, AND DECLARES MINE-CLEARING VESSELS 'LEGITIMATE TARGETS.' BRITAIN AND FRANCE REFUSE TO LEAD THE NAVAL COALITION. REUTERS REPORTS UP TO 400 CHINESE MANPADS BOUND FOR IRAN WITHIN WEEKS; BEIJING CALLS IT 'COMPLETELY GROUNDLESS.' BRENT JUMPS BACK ABOVE $90. AND THE DRAFT RUNG FALLS FOR THE FIRST TIME IN THE WAR.

**Iran claims the strike it left unclaimed.** A day after CENTCOM announced an "attempted surprise attack" that Tehran neither acknowledged nor explained, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps stated that its air force had targeted Muwaffaq Salti Air Base and a CENTCOM centre in Jordan. Jordan's air defences intercepted five missiles. The IRGC framed the campaign as open-ended: "As long as threats against the Islamic Republic of Iran continue and illegal and vicious actions by American forces against our interests continue, the resistance will continue." No US casualties were reported. This is a material change in the record: the attribution is now bilateral where the previous cycle had only the American account, and Iran's four-day reciprocal halt is over on its own terms. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera read the timing — hours after the Trump-Netanyahu meeting — as Tehran "sending a message to Trump that they need to be involved in all discussions" and attempting to "retake the initiative and momentum."

**And it returned to the shipping lanes.** The IRGC said it had struck and stopped three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, claiming the vessels "continued to move along an unsafe and illegal route, ignoring our warnings"; Tasnim carried the item as "Three Trespassing Vessels Stopped in Strait of Hormuz." These are the first Iranian strikes on Hormuz shipping claimed since the two-sided halt began on July 24-26. No casualties were reported and no independent confirmation of damage was available through the cycle close. The strikes also formally satisfy the trigger Trump announced on July 22 — that the United States would bomb and destroy one Iranian bridge or power plant every time Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait, with targets potentially including those "located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran." That doctrine was not invoked by the cycle close.

**Trump's answer was categorical and unspecific.** He said Iran was "going to get a beating" for the attempted overnight missile attack and told Fox News "we'll be hitting them hard," repeating that the US had "destroyed most of" Iran and that he would "finish the job" by resuming strikes absent a deal. No target set, no date and no domain beyond the aerial was named — and no ground formation, amphibious operation or Kharg landing was mentioned by the President, the Pentagon or CENTCOM.

**What the United States actually did was strike Iraq — with Saudi aircraft alongside.** US Central Command announced that it "and the Saudi Arabian Armed Forces conducted precision strikes in Iraq, July 28, against Iran-aligned terrorists that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) directed to attack U.S. forces and Saudi energy infrastructure." The targets were multiple logistics hubs and weapons storage sites. CENTCOM cited more than 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the preceding 72 hours, none of which it said succeeded, and more than 600 attempted attacks on US personnel and facilities between February and April 2026. The Saudi participation is the threshold event: it is the first time Riyadh has claimed responsibility for launching strikes inside Iraq since the war began, and Gulf analysts described it as a milestone in US-Saudi military cooperation and the end of Riyadh's practice of keeping its military outside the American campaign. Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki confirmed coordination with CENTCOM, said the strikes hit militia positions directly linked to cross-border drone attacks, and reported that Saudi air defences had "intercepted and destroyed multiple drones launched from Iraqi territory aimed at vital petroleum facilities in the Kingdom's Eastern Province and Riyadh region." The defence ministry invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, asserted the Kingdom's "right to self-defence," said it "does not seek escalation but will respond to any aggression it faces," and reserved the right to respond "at the appropriate time and place."

**The cost was borne in Iraq, and Baghdad objected on sovereignty grounds.** Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces said at least 20 of its members were killed and 32 wounded, with strike sites reported across Baghdad, Wasit, Nineveh, Basra, Kirkuk, Karbala and Diyala provinces, and condemned "a highly dangerous escalation" violating Iraqi sovereignty and "official security institutions." The Iraqi presidency "categorically rejected any attacks in Iraqi territory" while also opposing "the use of Iraqi territory as a launching point" — a formulation that rejects the strike while conceding the grievance behind it. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi convened an emergency security meeting. Iran's foreign ministry condemned "aggressive attacks" violating Iraq's "national sovereignty and territorial integrity." Whether the operation hit IRGC-directed proxy infrastructure or elements of Iraq's own legally constituted security apparatus cannot be settled from open sources: the PMF is formally both, and no target list or damage assessment has been published. See open-questions: us-saudi-iraq-strikes-pmf-status-july-2026.

**The Hormuz governance track went backwards, and it is now priced.** Iran rejected the Gulf-backed Omani proposal outright. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi described what was offered: "Oman proposed to us the creation of a route in the Strait of Hormuz, with 50 percent of it located in our territorial waters and 50 percent in Omani territorial waters" — ships entering through Iranian waters and exiting through Omani, funded by voluntary industry contributions on the Strait of Malacca model, which generates roughly $70 million a year. Iran's counterproposal inverts it: "Our proposal is for one route to lie entirely within the territorial waters of the Islamic Republic of Iran, with part of the other route also passing through Iranian territorial waters," giving Tehran oversight of both inbound and outbound traffic, with a reported $1 million per ship "service fee" earmarked for reconstruction. He tied the demand to war aims — "If the Strait of Hormuz returns to its previous state, our success in this war is not complete" — argued the June 17 MOU obliged Iran to provide free safe passage "for only 60 days," and denied Iran had sought talks: "there was no begging from the Iranian delegation to continue the negotiations," with Tehran stating it had not requested direct negotiations with Washington in fifteen days. Washington's position is unchanged — "Iran cannot toll the Strait, which is an international waterway," under "existing international law." Reporting now describes US-Iran negotiations as stalled.

**Iran's sharpest threat of the cycle was aimed at the coalition, not at troops.** Gharibabadi: "We told them explicitly that under no circumstances are they permitted to do so… if they bring equipment or any vessel… for mine-clearing operations near the Strait of Hormuz, they will be considered legitimate targets." Demining, he said, is Iran's own responsibility, and US warships are not permitted near the Strait. That statement attacks the core premise of the mission Washington is trying to raise — and the mission cannot presently find its leadership. POLITICO reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is urging the United Kingdom and France to help lead the naval coalition, with UK Defence Minister Wes Streeting assisting, and that European allies are refusing to support it "until they see an enduring ceasefire in the Iran war." Four British officials and one US official, all anonymous, said no movement was expected soon. The planned London conference is intended to establish operational roles and determine which nations would contribute warships for mine-clearing and civilian shipping protection; the report characterises the effort as the most concerted US attempt to seek allied assistance since the war began.

**A reported Chinese arms transfer enters the file.** Reuters reported, citing three sources familiar with the deal, that Iran is expected to receive within weeks the first shipment of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defence launchers — 300 to 400 QW-12 and FN-16 infrared-guided MANPADS worth $60-70 million, contracted through the Hong Kong-based intermediary Zhongqing Baoshang International Investment and routed from Urumqi in western China through Pakistan. It would be Tehran's largest known effort to rebuild the short-range air defences the war exposed as inadequate. China's foreign ministry called the report "completely groundless" and said China "has consistently played a role in promoting peace and ending the conflict"; Pakistan's military called the claims "absolutely concocted and false"; the intermediary's parent group did not respond to requests for comment. No interdiction, imagery, manifest, delivery or sanctions designation has been reported. Recorded as contested, not confirmed — see open-questions: china-manpads-transfer-iran-july-2026.

**Markets and the Strait.** Brent reversed and crossed back above $90: the straits.live tracker showed $90.40, up 3.43% (+$3.00) over 24 hours at 23:03Z, with a 7-day range of $101.47 to $82.51, and CNBC headlined "Brent oil jumps back above $90 after Trump threatens to hit Iran hard" after reporting a July 28 close of $84.09, down 4.8%. The move ends a three-session slide that had taken roughly $14 off the July 23 settle of $100.69. Pump prices moved the other way and the decoupling is now visible in both directions: AAA's national average was $4.0910 for regular, down fractionally, and $5.3290 for diesel — another war high, having risen on every day of the crude decline. The Strait eased a second day from a still-closed baseline: 339 vessels anchored or stopped (down from 405), 68 tankers running dark (down from 77), with IMF PortWatch's most recent count still 10 commercial transits on July 23 against an 88-per-day pre-crisis baseline — about 11% of normal — and the tracker's closure day count at 151. Convoys move only under naval escort, and UN News continues to report stranded seafarers trapped aboard.

**Casualties and attrition.** A Pentagon official said that "because Operation Epic Fury has concluded, the military has decided to classify casualties tied to the latest strikes in the new category," and would not offer a date for the operation's formal end; total wounded across the Operation Epic Fury and "Overseas Operations" categories now stands at 642. The four reclassified deaths are the three soldiers killed when Iranian ballistic missiles and drones struck a base in Jordan on July 17 and one killed in Iraq on July 18 during a controlled detonation of an Iranian drone. Spokespeople continue to attribute the data changes to "anomalies" and "temporary data disruptions" rather than concealment. On the Iranian side the standing HRANA cumulative baseline is 3,636 deaths (1,221 military, 1,701 civilian, 714 unclassified) against the Foundation of Martyrs' 3,468, with US and Israeli estimates at 6,000 or more and injured estimates ranging from 15,000 to the Iranian Health Ministry's 26,500. Political executions since February 28 reached at least 50 with public hangings in Isfahan on July 28 — a toll distinct from war casualties. Reported interceptor depletion is unchanged: more than 11,000 munitions expended in the first sixteen days, with Patriot and THAAD stocks three or more years from restoration — and Kyiv is now bidding for the same magazine, having offered Ukrainian drone-countermeasure expertise in exchange for Patriots at the Oval Office.

**Ground-invasion indicators — zero for a 154th day, and two preconditions moved backward.** This is the cleanest negative cycle of the war: escalation resumed on the ballistic, maritime and proxy-air rungs while the ground rung not only failed to move but had two of its structural preconditions regress. First, the draft. On July 23 the Selective Service System withdrew the proposed rules for automatic draft registration it had submitted to the White House on March 30, after the White House held them for nearly four months without acting and without comment. The statutory mandate is unchanged — automatic registration must still begin on December 19, 2026 under the December 2025 law, and the agency is separately reported to be procuring a draft mobilisation simulator — but no implementing rule is now pending, and the agency must either complete multiple administrative proceedings before the deadline or Congress must postpone or rescind it. Every prior data point on this indicator pointed one way; this is the first reversal. Automatic registration was never a draft: it automates the register should one be called, and no draft has been called, no lottery scheduled and no induction machinery activated. Second, allied force generation: the only force generation actually under way in this war is a naval escort coalition, and both governments Washington asked to lead it declined. Meanwhile the American response to Iranian escalation was an air strike on a proxy in a third country flown jointly with Saudi aircraft — coalition-building in the air domain, not ground mobilisation. Iran's own declared tripwire is anti-shipping and anti-minesweeping rather than anti-landing, and its war aim at the chokepoint is administrative control and transit revenue. The amphibious picture is unchanged seven days on: USNI News's July 27 tracker places USS Boxer (LHD-4) in the Arabian Sea with USS Comstock (LSD-45), USS Portland (LPD-27) and the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit, alongside expeditionary sea base USS Miguel Keith (ESB-5) and independently deployed destroyers USS Milius (DDG-69), USS Michael Murphy (DDG-112) and USS John Finn (DDG-113); The War Zone's July 28 count confirms the Boxer ARG as the sole deployed amphibious ready group fleet-wide; USS Tripoli (LHA-7) remains home in Sasebo after disembarking 31st MEU elements at Okinawa on July 22, with no relief ARG announced. Carriers Abraham Lincoln and George H.W. Bush remain in the CENTCOM area of responsibility, George Washington (CVN-73) is in the South China Sea, and Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) is leading RIMPAC 2026 near Hawaii. Kharg Island remains fortified, repeatedly struck from the air, and unseized. Force levels hold at roughly 50,000. Foreign Policy's July 24 survey of former US military officials remains the standing expert assessment that the United States "does not appear to be moving toward a major ground operation in Iran," with retired Gen. Joseph Votel limiting the plausible case to "the use of ground forces in limited raids that are going after key locations." The domestic permission structure is at its weakest of the conflict: Reuters/Ipsos found 33% approve and 62% disapprove of US attacks on Iran, with nearly 70% saying the goals have not been explained. **The predicted US ground seizure of Hormuz/Kharg remains DISCONFIRMED.**

**Other theatres (July 28-29, 2026).** *Gulf:* the Houthis fired ballistic missiles at the Saudi state-owned product tanker NCC Ghazal, with spokesman Yahya Saree citing "violation of the maritime embargo imposed on the Saudi enemy" and the vessel reversing course; UKMTO confirmed an explosion with the crew safe. The 'Bahrain Shield' exercise ran July 28-30 with the armed forces of all six GCC states. The World Bank's 2026 GCC growth forecast remains cut from 4.4% to 1.3%, with roughly 80 energy facilities hit and about $58bn of damage. *Russia-Ukraine:* the Senate advanced the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by 86-12, hours after Graham's funeral and after Zelensky's closed-door appeal to senators, which he watched from the gallery; the bill authorises tariffs of up to 200% on the largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, and expands sanctions on Russian banks, elites, oligarchs and the shadow fleet. Ukraine's General Staff recorded 226 clashes on July 28 with Pokrovsk hottest at 29 assaults, against 59 airstrikes with 190 guided bombs, 6,125 kamikaze drones and 2,047 attacks on positions. Zelensky said on July 27 that Russia is preparing Voronezh Oblast bases for approximately 30,000 additional North Korean soldiers atop an estimated 15,000 already deployed. *Latin America:* Venezuela's formal transition talks open August 1 between a delegation led by acting president Delcy Rodríguez and a Machado-less opposition group, with rival marches in Caracas on July 28 and leftist demonstrators saying Rodríguez negotiates "with a gun to her head"; Cuba suffered its fourth island-wide grid collapse of 2026, leaving all ten million inhabitants without power, and called Colombia's incoming severance of ties an "act of subordination" to Washington, as President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella prepares to close 14 embassies and 15 consulates on taking office August 7. *US-China:* the reported MANPADS transfer sits beside an intact diplomatic calendar — Xi's White House visit is still expected around September 24, and USTR has extended tariff exclusions on 178 Chinese products to November 10, 2026, with the July 24 Section 301 forced-labour duties fully operative since the in-transit window closed July 28. *DPRK:* satellite imagery from July 21 shows renovated facilities at Sohae ahead of North Korea's first military reconnaissance-satellite launch since 2024, and Lavrov said on July 22 that Russia no longer supports Korean Peninsula denuclearisation; PRC-DPRK trade reached $1.5bn in H1 2026, the highest since 2017. *Hormuz-affected economies:* Japan draws close to three-quarters of its oil imports through the Strait, South Korea roughly 60% of its crude, and India almost half its crude and about 60% of its gas; Qatar and the UAE supply 99% of Pakistan's LNG, 72% of Bangladesh's and 53% of India's.
