### Iran Fires on a Cargo Vessel Near Oman; UN IMO Pauses Its Hormuz Ship-Shepherding Program (June 25, 2026)

The week's de-escalation reversed on the maritime track. A cargo ship reported it was struck on its starboard side by a projectile about **7.5 nautical miles southeast of Oman's port of Dahit;** a **US official told Reuters that Iran was behind the attack.** In response, the **UN International Maritime Organization (IMO) paused the program it had been running to shepherd and evacuate ships and seafarers through the Strait of Hormuz,** and **Iran's IRGC Navy warned that safe passage would be permitted only via routes designated by Tehran** and that vessels violating its transit instructions would **"face action."** The strike — the first Iranian fire on shipping in several days — was Tehran beginning to enforce by fire the sovereignty/authorization claim it had asserted verbally earlier in the week, and it reignited fears over the durability of the interim deal even as the deal, the lifted blockade, and the 60-day roadmap all remained formally in effect.

*Sources:* CBC News, "Ship evacuation in Strait of Hormuz paused following attack on cargo vessel," June 25, 2026; NBC News, "U.N. agency pauses Strait of Hormuz evacuation effort as ship struck off Oman," June 25, 2026; CBS News live updates, "Iran strikes vessel in Strait of Hormuz amid debate over transit fees," June 25, 2026; The Times of Israel live blog, "Iran fired on cargo ship in Hormuz, US officials tell Reuters," June 25, 2026.

### Oil Reverses Its Slide and Rises on the Strike (June 25, 2026)

Oil prices, which had fallen to a war-period low — WTI briefly under $70 on June 24 — **turned around and rose to session highs** after the attack. **West Texas Intermediate futures rose more than 2% to settle at $71.92/bbl,** while **International Brent climbed 2.1% to $75.26,** as the strike "refueled fears that tensions in the Middle East could stay elevated." The reversal partially retraced the war-period low and confirms a live residual risk premium, but it left oil far below the early-2026 wartime peaks above $110 and well under the sustained $130+ a US ground commitment would imply.

*Sources:* CNBC, "Oil reverses losses, rises after an Iran attack on cargo vessel," June 25, 2026.

### Nuclear-Inspections Dispute Widens — Grossi Says Inspections "Going to Happen"; Iran Says Only After a Final Deal (June 24, 2026)

The parallel verification dispute widened. **IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi** gave his firmest statement yet that inspectors would visit Iran's enrichment sites under the interim deal: the accord "says explicitly that the nuclear activities that are going to be carried out with regards to the nuclear material facilities will be supervised by the IAEA — in all letters," and "obviously, to do that, we will have to inspect"; "whether this happens the day after tomorrow or in one week or in 10 days, it's important, but not essential. **This is going to happen.**" Iranian deputy foreign minister **Kazem Gharibabadi** pushed back, saying any such visit would come **"only within the framework of a final agreement and as a result of practical action by the other side to end all sanctions,"** and noting that **Tehran did not meet Grossi while in Switzerland.** Since the 2025 war the IAEA has been blocked from Iran's enrichment sites; the two governments have repeatedly disagreed in public about what the signed document requires. The dispute is a verification clash negotiated in the open, not a ground indicator.

*Sources:* NPR, "Dispute widens over Iran nuclear inspections," June 24, 2026; PBS NewsHour, "Dispute over nuclear inspections shows how U.S. and Iran are negotiating in public," June 24, 2026; US News/AP, June 24, 2026.

### Senate Walks Back Its War-Powers Rebuke of Trump (June 23-24, 2026)

On **June 23 the Senate passed a war-powers resolution 50-48** directing the president to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran absent a declaration of war or specific congressional authorization — the first time such a measure had cleared both chambers (the House passed its version earlier in June). Four Republicans (Cassidy, Collins, Murkowski, Paul) joined all but one Democrat (Fetterman voted no). **One day later the Senate reversed course:** a procedural motion to advance a similar resolution by Democratic Sen. **Tim Kaine failed 50-47 on June 24,** after Trump pressed Republicans who had backed or missed the first vote. **Sens. Cassidy and Paul flipped** (Cassidy voting against, Paul voting "present"); only Collins and Murkowski still backed advancing it. The resolutions are non-binding and will not be sent to the White House; Trump hailed the second vote as putting Iran "on notice." The episode lowered a near-term legislative constraint on the president's war powers but ordered no movement of forces.

*Sources:* CNN Politics, "War powers resolution: Senate votes to walk back rebuke of Trump over Iran," June 24, 2026; CBS News, "Senate rejects measure to restrict Trump's Iran war powers as key Republicans shift votes," June 24, 2026; Time, June 24, 2026; NPR, June 23, 2026.

### Lebanon Ceasefire Stays Fragile (June 24-25, 2026)

The **June 19 US/Qatar/Iran-mediated Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire** remained the live regional fault line. Israeli strikes continued in southern Lebanon and **Hezbollah demanded a full Israeli withdrawal** as a condition of the truce, with the cumulative Lebanon toll since March 2 near 4,000 killed and more than a million displaced. Israel is not a party to the US-Iran deal, and the Israel-Lebanon track (a separate Washington negotiation) stayed unresolved.

*Sources:* Al Jazeera, "Israel continues attacks on Lebanon despite agreeing to ceasefire," June 19-24, 2026; Time, June 4-24, 2026.

### Hormuz Governance/Tolls Dispute and Rubio's Gulf Tour (June 24, 2026)

As the 60-day Bürgenstock roadmap proceeded, the question of who governs the reopened Strait of Hormuz hardened into a second running dispute alongside the nuclear-inspections clash. Secretary of State **Marco Rubio** opened a Gulf tour in the **United Arab Emirates** on June 24, called his consultations with Gulf partners **"frank,"** and said the next round of US-Iran technical talks would convene **"next week" in Geneva.** On the Strait he drew the firmest US line yet against Iranian transit charges: **"It's an international waterway. No country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway,"** adding that if Iran tries to propose tolls **"there's not going to be a final deal,"** and framing Strait security as a matter for **Iran and the Gulf Coast Coalition** to settle within a security framework.

Iran pressed the opposite position. Chief negotiator and parliament speaker **Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf** said the Strait **"will never return to its pre-war conditions and will be administered by the Islamic Republic of Iran, in accordance with international law,"** even though both sides had agreed on June 22 to a communications mechanism to keep the waterway open. Iran's **Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA)** said its planned fees for transiting ships would be **suspended for the duration of the 60-day MOU window** — a deferral, not an abandonment, of the toll claim. Tehran is permitting **toll-free transit** during that window.

On the maritime picture itself, tanker traffic held near its war-period high — **109 vessels Saturday-Monday** and **~25 ships the prior Thursday** (13 west-to-east, 12 east-to-west) — still a fraction of the pre-war ~120-130/day. The **northern (Iranian) and southern (Omani) routes are open;** the **central channel remains closed pending ~80 mines.** Oil read continued de-escalation: **Brent fell below ~$74/bbl on June 24,** its lowest since late February, as rising traffic and talks progress eased supply fears — far below the early-2026 wartime peaks above $110 and the sustained $130+ that a US ground commitment would imply. The **US naval blockade stayed lifted (Day 7).**

The **nuclear-inspections dispute carried over:** Trump posted that Iran had **"fully and completely agreed to highest level Nuclear inspections long into the future,"** reprising Vance's June 22 claim, while Iran's Foreign Ministry continued to deny any meeting with IAEA chief Grossi and any scheduled inspection of the sites the US bombed in 2025. **Lebanon's June 19 ceasefire stayed the live fault line** — Israel continued strikes in southern Lebanon and **Hezbollah demanded a full Israeli withdrawal** as a condition of the truce (cumulative toll near 4,000 since March 2; Israel is not a party to the US-Iran deal).

The **ground rung was unchanged and de-escalatory on the US side:** no US troops in Iran, no Kharg Island assault, no new amphibious ready group or Marine Expeditionary Unit order, no draft; the blockade stays lifted and the USS Boxer ARG stays disaggregated. The day's escalation levers were diplomatic (the Hormuz-tolls and IAEA-inspections disputes), not ground. Who ultimately governs the Strait and whether Iran can levy any charge is **CONTESTED-UNRESOLVED** (open-questions: iran-hormuz-administration-tolls-dispute-june-2026).

### US-Iran Dispute Over Nuclear Inspections — Vance/Trump Say Iran Agreed; Iran Denies Any Scheduled IAEA Visit (June 23, 2026)

The day-old roadmap's first open friction centered on whether Iran had agreed to readmit international inspectors. VP JD Vance said on June 22 that "the Iranians have agreed to invite IAEA inspectors back into their country," with the agency due "this week." On June 23 Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran that no meeting with IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi had taken place in Switzerland and that UN inspectors were not scheduled to examine the nuclear sites the US bombed in 2025. President Trump insisted Iran "will agree to have major weapons inspections in order to ensure nuclear honesty long into [the] future" "despite their protestations and false statements to the contrary," and told reporters that if Iran had not agreed to inspections he would cut off talks "immediately," posting that without the concession "there would be no further negotiations!" Whether Iran actually committed is contested and unresolvable from open sources until inspectors do or do not enter the country (Washington Post, "Iran says no to nuclear inspections, countering Vance statement," June 23, 2026; CNN, "Trump keeps claiming Iran made concessions. Iran keeps denying them," June 23, 2026; NPR; PBS NewsHour; NBC News, June 23, 2026).

### Talks Continue Despite the Dispute; Pezeshkian Meets Pakistani Mediators (June 23-24, 2026)

The inspections dispute did not break the roadmap. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian met Pakistani officials mediating the negotiations while US and Iranian technical teams continued detail work following the Switzerland session; a further round was reported for June 23-25 in Washington. The episode sharpened the standing open question of whether the 60-day roadmap is genuine consolidation of the June 17 settlement or another deferral in a long series of US-claimed-then-Iran-denied concessions (NPR, "A U.S.-Iran dispute over nuclear inspections clouds work to finalize a war-ending deal," June 23, 2026; CBS News live blog, June 23, 2026).

### Iran Asserts Hormuz Sovereignty; Tanker Traffic Hits a War-Period High (June 22-23, 2026)

Tehran said ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz would now require its authorization and signaled it could levy transit charges through a compulsory-insurance framework — a sovereignty assertion sitting alongside the June 22 communications channel meant to keep the strait open. Traffic nonetheless rose to its highest since the conflict began at end-February: 109 vessels transited Saturday through Monday, still below the pre-war ~120-130/day, with a backlog of hundreds awaiting passage and the central channel still being de-mined. The US naval blockade remained lifted; the contest over the chokepoint runs through maritime law and toll politics, the structural inverse of a US ground seizure (Times of Israel, "Contradicting Vance, Iran says no plans for IAEA inspections, asserts sovereignty at Hormuz," June 23, 2026; AOL / Fox Business, "Oil tanker traffic through Strait of Hormuz hits highest level since conflict began but mines remain," June 22-23, 2026; CNBC).

Brent crude fell about 4% to $77.39 on June 22 after Vance reported progress in the Iran talks and confirmed the Strait of Hormuz remained open, then eased further to around $75/bbl on June 23 (down ~0.3% on the day and ~4.5% over five days) — far below the early-2026 wartime peaks above $110. ### Lebanon Ceasefire Holds Tensely; Lebanon Backs the Deconfliction Cell but Ties It to an Israeli Withdrawal (June 22-24, 2026)

The renewed Israel-Hezbollah truce held into a second day, but Israeli strikes continued and Hezbollah responded. Lebanon welcomed the US/Iran/Lebanon deconfliction cell created at Bürgenstock — Araghchi's "1st real test" — but officials said any such mechanism must lead to a lasting ceasefire and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from occupied Lebanese territory. Israeli FM Gideon Saar said Israel would "respect the ceasefire in Lebanon as long as it won't be breached by Hezbollah" and would not withdraw from the security zone. Because Israel is not a party to the US-Iran deal, on-the-ground enforcement of the Lebanon truce remains the central durability risk (Al Jazeera, "Lebanon discusses deconfliction mechanism ahead of Israel talks," June 22, 2026; Arab News, "Lebanon backs deconfliction cell proposal, but ties support to Israeli withdrawal," June 22-23, 2026; The Inquirer/AP, June 22, 2026).

### Postponed Swiss Technical Talks Reconvene at Bürgenstock; Vance Claims "Great Progress" (June 21, 2026)

The in-person US-Iran technical talks postponed Friday went ahead on Sunday June 21 at the Bürgenstock resort on Lake Lucerne — a quadrilateral session with the United States (Vice President JD Vance), Iran (Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf) and mediators Pakistan and Qatar present. A first session ran roughly 80 minutes and broke around 15:00 GMT for internal consultations, and an "emergency session" on the fighting in Lebanon was added to the agenda. Vance claimed "great progress" within the first hours and framed the goal as turning "over a new leaf." The talks are technical — implementing the June 17 memorandum of understanding and opening a 60-day nuclear/sanctions track — and produced no final agreement at the time of this update; the postponed process thus reconvened rather than collapsing. (Al Jazeera, "'High drama' over Trump threats and Lebanon at US-Iran talks in Switzerland"; "Vance wants to 'turn over a new leaf'..."; CBS News live blog, "U.S. and Iranian negotiators meet as Trump threatens..."; Wikipedia, "2025-2026 Iran-United States negotiations," June 21, 2026.)

### US Disputes Iran's Hormuz Closure — CENTCOM: "Traffic Continues to Flow" (June 20-21, 2026)

The United States rejected Iran's June 20 closure declaration outright. CENTCOM stated that "Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic continues to flow," and the US said 55 merchant ships carrying more than 17 million barrels of oil transited the strait on Saturday June 20. Vance said Iran had not fired on shipping for a second consecutive night, calling it evidence Tehran is "honoring their end of the commitment." The status of the strait is thus disputed — a declared Iranian closure against continued (if still-reduced) flow — rather than a hard closure, and the US naval blockade itself remained lifted. Independent real-time verification of transit volumes through the contested chokepoint is not available in open sources, leaving the closure-vs-flow dispute unresolved in this window. (CNN live, June 20, 2026; CBS News live blog, June 21, 2026.)

### Escalatory Rhetoric Alongside the Talks; Tolls Dispute Stays Open (June 20-21, 2026)

Even as negotiators met, the rhetoric sharpened. Trump threatened to "hit Iran very hard again," said Iran "won't have a country," and (per CBS) vowed to "blow the [expletive] out of them" if the deal fails; Ghalibaf countered that "we don't count on the threats of the Americans" and said Iran's armed forces are "ready to respond in another way," warning the US to "be careful with their statements." On the tolls dispute, Trump wrote on Truth Social that there will be "NO tolls after the 60 day period has expired, unless they are imposed by and for the United States of America... for services rendered as the Guardian Angel to the countries of the Middle East" — vowing Iran will not charge Hormuz tolls but signaling the US might, while Iran maintains any transit fees are a sovereignty matter to be managed with Oman. (NPR; CBS News; Al Jazeera; Fortune; The Hill, June 20-21, 2026.)

### Renewed Lebanon Ceasefire Repeatedly Violated — ~145 Killed Over Two Days (June 20-21, 2026)

The US/Qatar/Iran-mediated Israel-Hezbollah truce renewed Friday June 19 did not hold: Israel struck numerous sites across Lebanon, with the death toll rising by roughly 145 over two days; Israel said Hezbollah fired more than 50 projectiles (Hezbollah denied it). The cumulative Lebanon toll from Israeli strikes is above 4,000 since March 2, with more than a million displaced (over 20% of the population); Israeli troops remain in the southern security zone and Netanyahu has refused to withdraw. The Lebanon file was the explicit "emergency" agenda item added at the Swiss talks, underscoring that it remains the deal's live fault line. (CBS News; PBS News, "Israel and Hezbollah renew ceasefire..."; Wikipedia, "2026 Lebanon war," June 20-21, 2026.)

**Russia-Ukraine:** After Ukraine's June 18 strike on Moscow's Kapotnya (Moscow Oil) refinery — the largest attack on the capital since 2022, with 190 drones reportedly downed approaching the city and Moscow airports suspended — Ukraine struck an oil terminal in occupied Crimea overnight June 21, extending its deep-strike energy campaign. On the ground, Kostiantynivka has become Russia's main objective (Russian forces entered its northeastern part and achieved a tactical breakthrough in the west, advancing along the T-0504); formal peace talks remain frozen (the Kremlin rejected new talks; Zelenskyy issued five conditions to the E3 in London). **Colombia:** the June 21 presidential runoff was won narrowly by far-right newcomer Abelardo de la Espriella over leftist Senator Iván Cepeda (~49.65% vs. ~48.70%, a ~0.95-point margin on the highest turnout since 1998); de la Espriella, endorsed by Trump and Flávio Bolsonaro, takes office August 7 — a rightward shift. **Venezuela:** the Rodríguez government keeps granting US-brokered oil concessions (PDVSA-Shell), and the Maduro/Flores Manhattan hearing stays set for July 22. **Cuba:** the fuel/energy/humanitarian emergency keeps deepening under the US oil blockade. **US-China:** Beijing is positioned as an Iran-war diplomatic beneficiary — FM Wang Yi urged Iran's Araghchi that Hormuz be "properly handled," and CNN ran "China is counting its wins from the Iran war" (June 20); trade holds at ~30% tariffs under a 60-day pause, with a new USTR 12.5% Section 301 tariff proposed. **DPRK:** quiet in the window (latest activity the June 15 modular-launcher and tactical-cruise-missile test). **Hormuz-exposed importers:** Japan expects ~100% of July crude from non-Hormuz sources (Takaichi), India is ~70% non-Hormuz with record Russian-crude imports (~2.66M bpd June 1-19), Pakistan cut petrol by Rs74/L while co-mediating the Swiss talks, and parts of Europe (Slovenia rationing; Austria fuel-tax cuts) continued relief measures. ### Ground Rung — Still De-escalatory on the US Side; the Weekend's Moves Were Diplomatic and Drawdown-Leaning (June 21-22, 2026)

Every ground-invasion execution indicator stayed at zero on the US side through the deal's most precarious weekend. The two US-side developments were diplomatic and drawdown-leaning, not ground moves: the postponed technical talks reconvened June 21 at Bürgenstock, and the USS Boxer amphibious ready group / 11th MEU (~4,000 Marines) was disaggregated despite earlier reporting it might join the war — a fresh de-escalation signal that removes amphibious mass rather than concentrating it for any landing. CENTCOM publicly disputed Iran's Hormuz closure ("traffic continues to flow"), and the US naval blockade itself remains lifted. The USS Tripoli (LHA-7) ARG / 31st MEU remains forward-deployed in a routine posture (explicitly not invasion staging), and the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group was earlier flagged as likely first to rotate out. No US ground troops are in Iran, no Kharg ground assault has been ordered or executed, no third ARG or new MEU has been ordered, there has been no BCT-scale Guard activation, and there is no draft/Selective Service signal; roughly 50,000 US troops remain in the CENTCOM area of responsibility. The escalation that did occur over the weekend was verbal and air-power-framed (Trump's "hit Iran very hard again"), never ground; the residual uncertainty is durability — the disputed Hormuz status, the violated Lebanon ceasefire, the open toll dispute — but every live failure mode points to the air/naval/missile register, not to US ground forces. (The War Zone, "America's Naval Force Posture Largely Unchanged..." and USS Boxer ARG reporting; armyrecognition.com; CBS News; CNN, June 15-21, 2026.)

### Iran's IRGC Re-Closes the Strait of Hormuz Over Israel's Lebanon Strikes (June 20, 2026)

Only four days after commercial transits resumed for the first time in roughly 110 days, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps declared the Strait of Hormuz closed again on June 20, tying the move to Israel's continued strikes on Lebanon, which Tehran casts as a breach of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding, and warning of "reciprocal action" if Washington does not honour its commitments. Crucially, the US naval blockade itself remained lifted — CENTCOM had said all blockade-enforcement efforts had "ceased" — so the new closure is an Iranian coercive maritime measure, reversing the reopening from the Iranian side, not a return of the US interdiction campaign. The move echoed Iran's April 18 Supreme National Security Council re-closure (after the April 17 voluntary reopening), and ~80 million barrels of crude were reported lined up to exit the strait. (Al Jazeera, "Iran closes Strait of Hormuz as Pakistan says new talks with US due Sunday"; "Iran shuts Strait of Hormuz as Israel tests MOU with Lebanon strikes"; "Iran warns of reciprocal action if US doesn't honour MOU commitments"; oilprice.com, June 20, 2026.)

### Postponed Swiss Technical Talks Set to Reconvene; Vance Departs; Iran "Ready to Move Forward" (June 20-21, 2026)

Despite Friday's postponement, Vice President JD Vance departed for the technical US-Iran meeting at the Bürgenstock resort above Lake Lucerne, and Pakistan said a new round of talks was due Sunday June 21, with Pakistani, Saudi and Turkish mediators coordinating. Iran said it was "ready to move forward" with the deal provided Israel abides by its terms. The postponed process thus appeared to be reconvening rather than collapsing; as of this update, the outcome of the Sunday session had not yet been reported. (Al Jazeera, "IRGC says Strait of Hormuz closed; Vance leaves for technical Iran-US talks"; "Iran ready to move forward with US deal, says Israel must abide by terms," June 19-20, 2026.)

One day after the Trump-brokered Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire renewal, Israeli strikes killed at least 32 people in Lebanon on June 20, which Al Jazeera reported was "putting US-Iran talks in peril." MSF said conditions in the southern city of Nabatieh resembled a "death trap"; the UK condemned an Israeli minister over "inflammatory" Lebanon remarks; and the cumulative Lebanon toll since March 2 stood near 4,000 killed. Iran cited the continued Israeli operations as its reason for re-closing Hormuz, and the United States announced a new round of Israel-Lebanon talks in Washington the following week. (Al Jazeera, "Israeli strikes kill 32 in Lebanon, putting US-Iran talks in peril"; "US announces new round of Israel-Lebanon talks in Washington next week"; Middle East Eye, June 19-20, 2026.)

### Toll Dispute, $80B Pentagon Request, and Oil (June 19-20, 2026)

On the toll dispute, Trump vowed Iran would not be permitted to charge tolls on Hormuz traffic but said the US itself might; reporting indicated the MOU does not rule out future US tolls after an initial 60-day toll-free period. The Pentagon told lawmakers it needs roughly $80 billion for the Iran war and other expenses — a budget/sustainment request, not a mobilization or ground-deployment order — and Al Jazeera examined whether Trump must submit the Iran MOU to Congress. Oil rose on June 19 as Lebanon fighting erupted and Hormuz traffic stayed slow, with Brent near $80/bbl and WTI near $77, then held in that band as the June 20 re-closure added fresh war-risk premium — far below the early-2026 wartime peaks above $110. ### In-Person Swiss Follow-On Talks Postponed; Vance Cancels His Trip (June 19, 2026)

Switzerland's foreign ministry confirmed on Friday June 19 that the planned Bürgenstock meeting of the United States, Iran, Qatar and Pakistan "has been postponed," without specifying a new date, while preparatory work reportedly continued at the resort. The White House said Vice President JD Vance was no longer traveling to Switzerland, citing unresolved logistics ("the logistics of these negotiations have never been simple or predictable"); Iran had delayed sending its delegation over Israel's continued military operations in Lebanon. The interim memorandum of understanding signed electronically on June 17 remains in effect — the blockade stays lifted and Hormuz keeps reopening — but the 60-day window of broader nuclear and sanctions talks it was meant to open did not formally begin. CNBC framed it as the accord's first stumble ("hits early snag after Swiss talks fail to proceed as planned"). (CBS News; CNBC; Swiss Foreign Ministry / SWI swissinfo.ch; Al Jazeera, June 18-19, 2026.)

### Lebanon Flare-Up Nearly Derails the Deal — Then Trump Brokers a Ceasefire Renewal (June 19, 2026)

A sharp Lebanon escalation briefly threatened the whole accord. Israeli airstrikes killed at least 16 people across Lebanon overnight and the IDF reported four of its soldiers killed in fighting in the south, pushing the cumulative Lebanon toll since March 2 to roughly 4,000 dead. Iran — which had warned that Israeli operations in Lebanon would violate the US-Iran deal — delayed its Switzerland delegation, and the fighting "looked set to derail" the Washington-Tehran talks. Trump told NBC News in a phone call Friday afternoon that he had spoken with Israel and asked it to agree to a ceasefire; Israel and Hezbollah then agreed to renew their truce, with officials on both sides saying they would abide by it while warning against violations from the other. Netanyahu said Israel would respond forcefully to any Hezbollah violation and would retain "complete military freedom of action," and repeated that Israel will "not withdraw" from its southern-Lebanon security zone "as long as Israel's security needs require it" — capping the immediate fighting while leaving the underlying withdrawal dispute (Iran's resumption tripwire) unresolved. (NBC News; CNN live updates; CBS News, June 19, 2026.)

### Hormuz Reopening Continues but Stays a Trickle; Blockade Enforcement "Ceased" (June 18-19, 2026)

US Central Command said "American forces are not impeding the transit of vessels to or from Iranian ports" and that "all U.S. military blockade enforcement efforts have ceased"; sanctioned Iranian tankers entered the strait following the announcement, and Grimaldi Group, Cosco and Knutsen vessels were among those transiting. The reopening nonetheless remained far below normal: Lloyd's List estimated roughly 550 merchant ships still need to exit the Gulf, the main central route remains closed pending clearance of about 80 mines, and CNBC reiterated that full normalization is "weeks" away. (CBS News; CNBC; Lloyd's List, June 18-19, 2026.)

### Oil Steadies Near $80 on the Postponement; GOP Pushback on the Terms (June 19, 2026)

Brent crude steadied near $80/bbl on Friday — edging up from about $77 amid renewed uncertainty after the Swiss talks were postponed — but stayed on track for a sharp weekly decline as improving Hormuz shipping conditions kept unwinding the war-risk premium; the level is far below the early-2026 wartime peaks above $110. On the politics of the deal, Republican Senator Roger Wicker said he was "concerned that the memorandum... negotiates away the victories of Operation Epic Fury in ways that are completely out of step with the President's goals" — an intra-party critique that the war-ending terms concede too much, mirroring the war-powers pressure to end hostilities. (TradingEconomics; CNBC; CBS News live updates, June 19, 2026.)

### Deal Signed Electronically by Trump and Pezeshkian; Takes Immediate Effect; Friday Geneva Ceremony Cancelled (June 17-18, 2026)

President Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed the memorandum of understanding electronically Wednesday night — Trump at a candlelit dinner outside Paris during the G7 summit, Pezeshkian signing remotely — and the agreement took immediate effect. Because of the electronic signing, the in-person Friday June 19 ceremony in Geneva/Switzerland was cancelled, though negotiating teams still intend to convene at the Bürgenstock resort Friday to begin a 60-day window of broader talks on Iran's nuclear program and sanctions relief. The MOU extends the ceasefire, reopens the Strait of Hormuz, and lifts the US naval blockade. (Al Jazeera; CBS News; Business Standard, June 17-18, 2026.)

### US Naval Blockade Lifted by CENTCOM; Hormuz Reopening Begins — First Transits in ~110 Days (June 18, 2026)

US Central Command announced that the naval blockade of Iranian ports has been lifted "in accordance with the president's direction," with US military vessels remaining on station only to monitor compliance — physically ending the maritime-interdiction campaign that ran from April 13. Commercial traffic began returning to the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in roughly 110 days: maritime-intelligence firm Windward counted about 18 vessels transiting between 6 p.m. June 17 and 2 p.m. UTC June 18 (including a French-flagged LNG tanker, two Hong Kong-flagged tankers, an Italian-flagged vehicle carrier, a Japanese-controlled oil tanker, and Saudi-flagged tankers), which chief analyst Michelle Wiese Bockmann called "a sign of confidence in the agreement" that will "start as a trickle." CBS put Thursday-morning transits at "at least 10," and Lloyd's List called it the first transit in 110 days for major shipowners' vessels. Ships are using the northern (Iranian-waters) and southern (Omani-waters) routes while the main central route stays closed pending clearance of an estimated 80 mines; CNBC reported that full normalization of the backlog will take weeks. (CBS News; CNBC; Windward via Lloyd's List, June 18, 2026.)

### Vance: 12.5M Barrels Overnight — but "No Tolls or No Deal"; Iran and Oman Signal Hormuz Fees (June 18, 2026)

Vice President Vance said "12.5 million barrels of oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz last night," a war-era high, and warned that if Iran "tries to propose tolls," there is "not going to be a final deal" on the strait. This collides with Iran's signal (per Al Jazeera) that it will "charge fees for services" at the strait, managed jointly with Oman — contradicting Trump's pledge of permanently toll-free passage and forming the next likely friction point inside the 60-day window. Brent crude held a three-month-plus low near $77/bbl, continuing to unwind the war-risk premium. (CBS News; Al Jazeera; TradingEconomics, June 17-18, 2026.)

### Lebanon Stays the Live Fault Line; Netanyahu "Will Not Withdraw"; Toll ~3,912 (June 18, 2026)

The MOU calls for an "immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon," but Prime Minister Netanyahu declared Israel will "not withdraw from" its security zone in southern Lebanon; Iran's foreign minister said Israeli forces remaining would violate the agreement; and Hezbollah claimed it repelled Israeli advances Thursday. Lebanon's toll reached nearly 4,000 — 3,912 killed (Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health) and 11,873 wounded since March 2 — with Israeli losses at 31 soldiers and one civilian contractor since March 2, and one more soldier killed and seven wounded Thursday. The Trump administration briefed congressional leaders Thursday, where GOP Senator Roger Wicker expressed concern the deal "negotiates away" the military's victories. (CBS News live updates, June 18, 2026.)

Every ground-invasion execution indicator stayed at zero, and the consummation of the deal pushed the posture to its most de-escalatory point of the war. No US ground troops are in Iran, no Kharg ground assault has been ordered or executed, no third ARG or new MEU has been ordered, there has been no BCT-scale Guard activation, and there is no draft/Selective Service signal. Roughly 50,000 US troops remain in the CENTCOM area of responsibility with no net change; the USS Tripoli ARG / 31st MEU and three carrier strike groups remain on station, and the 82nd Airborne forward HQ is now a fading standing forcible-entry contingency as the blockade-lift and force-withdrawal clauses take effect. Decisively, the only US escalation levers still on the table — Trump's "restart the bombing campaign" threat and Vance's "no tolls or no deal" on Hormuz — are air/naval and diplomatic, not a ground push; the blockade is physically lifted, US forces are to withdraw, and the chokepoint is reopening by negotiated mine-clearing, the executed inverse of the predicted Hormuz/Kharg seizure. The disconfirmation is strong but not yet airtight on durability (the central route is still mined, the toll/fee dispute is open, and the Lebanon track is unresolved) — but a collapse over any of these would return the conflict to the air/naval/missile register, not vindicate a ground invasion. (Derived from CENTCOM/CBS coverage; prior force-posture reporting, June 18-19, 2026.)

### Deal Survives the Close of the G7: Trump Defends "the Trump Deal," Threatens to "Restart Bombing"; Full Text Still Unreleased (June 17, 2026)

Wrapping his final day at the G7 summit in the French Alps, President Trump held a news conference defending the 14-point agreement aimed at ending the conflict with Iran, calling it "the Trump deal." He said the agreement includes statements that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon and that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen, and warned that if Iran does not abide by the agreement the United States "may restart its bombing campaign" — an air-power threat, explicitly not a ground operation. G7 leaders threw their support behind the tentative deal, with French President Emmanuel Macron calling it "a very good deal" that "puts a stop to a situation of great instability that had terrible consequences for our economies." But no MOU text had been released publicly days after a senior US official's "within 24-48 hours" pledge; officials and reporting continued to describe the roughly page-and-a-half document as essentially a commitment to negotiate, opening a second phase of direct talks on Iran's nuclear program with no stated plan yet to deal with Iran's nuclear capabilities. The in-person signing remained set for Friday June 19 in Switzerland (the Swiss foreign ministry's Bürgenstock resort near Luzern; some reports still cited Geneva), with Vice President JD Vance — who has described the MOU as "about a page and a half" and "a very general document" — representing the United States. The deal calls for an immediate end to fighting in Lebanon between Israel and Hezbollah, but Israel's occupation of swaths of southern Lebanon remains one of its most delicate and unresolved elements. ### US and Iran Reach a Deal to End the War; Trump Authorizes Blockade Lift and Hormuz Reopening (June 14, 2026)

On Sunday June 14, President Trump and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif jointly announced that the United States and Iran had reached a deal to end the war, with Iranian state media broadcasting the announcement. Sharif posted on X that a peace deal "has been REACHED," adding that "both sides have declared the immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon." Trump wrote on Truth Social that "The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete... I hereby fully authorize the toll free opening of the Strait of Hormuz," and authorized "the immediate removal of the United States Naval blockade," adding "Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!" Iran's deputy foreign minister said the memorandum of understanding was complete and that the US naval blockade would end Sunday night; Defense Secretary Hegseth said the reopening would begin "immediately" but remained contingent on Iranian performance, targeting pre-war volumes within ~30 days, with Iran responsible for clearing its own mines (potentially into mid-2027).

Reported MOU terms (per US and Iranian accounts): a 60-day ceasefire extension; Hormuz reopened without transit tolls; the US lifting its naval blockade and withdrawing forces from the Gulf region (Iranian state TV left ambiguous whether this covers only war-deployed forces or pre-existing Gulf bases); a roughly 15-20 year Iranian uranium-enrichment lockout with nuclear-site dismantling (some steps immediate on signing, the rest negotiated over 60 days); and staggered relief of about $25 billion in frozen Iranian assets tied to compliance, with Trump insisting no money changes hands until Iran performs. A formal signing was set for Friday June 19 in Switzerland (reported as Geneva), to be executed electronically by Trump or in person by VP JD Vance.

The deal is not yet consummated: it remains unsigned until Friday, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's approval was not publicly confirmed, and earlier on June 14 Iran's IRGC-linked Fars News and Foreign Ministry had said "no text for a preliminary memorandum of understanding with the United States has been approved." It is already strained by the Lebanon track: Israel struck a Hezbollah command center in Beirut's Dahieh suburb and said it killed a senior Hezbollah commander in a "precise strike" in southern Lebanon around the announcement; Trump said "this morning's attack on Beirut should not have happened... at a time when we are so close to a Peace Deal"; Netanyahu told Trump Israel would not consider itself bound to halt operations in Lebanon and refused a Lebanon withdrawal commitment; Iran's parliament speaker warned the strikes could imperil the deal; and some oil tankers reportedly paused in the Strait. Markets read the deal as decisive de-escalation: WTI fell more than 4.5% to about $80 and Brent about 4% to about $83 as Sunday-evening trading opened — both their lowest since early March.

On the ground-invasion question the day was decisively de-escalatory: the deal would reopen Hormuz by negotiation and withdraw US forces — the structural inverse of an imminent ground invasion or resource seizure — with no US troops in Iran, no Kharg ground assault, no new ARG/MEU order, and no draft; the only US logistical movement remained four C-17s carrying signing-ceremony equipment to Europe for VP Vance's travel. (NBC News, "Deal reached between the United States and Iran, Trump says," June 14, 2026; PBS NewsHour, "Deal is reached to end Iran war and Trump orders stop to U.S. naval blockade," June 14, 2026; CBS News, June 14, 2026; Axios, June 14, 2026; Fox News; Jerusalem Post; Bloomberg; AOL/Yahoo Finance; ABC News; Times of Israel, June 14-15, 2026.)

### Trump Says the Deal Will Be Signed Sunday; Hormuz to Open "to All" Immediately After (June 13, 2026)

On Saturday June 13, President Trump posted on Truth Social that the agreement to end the war with Iran was "scheduled to get signed tomorrow, and immediately after it is signed, the Hormuz Strait is OPEN TO ALL," and that the deal would guarantee "long-term peace in the region." He framed it as the inverse of the Obama-era JCPOA — "My Agreement with Iran is the exact opposite, A WALL TO NO NUCLEAR WEAPON" — and said the Iranians "no longer want a Nuclear Weapon, nor will they have one." The signing was reported set for Europe (Geneva), with Vice President JD Vance plus negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attending and Trump saying he would not attend himself; four US Air Force C-17 transport planes had departed to Europe to move equipment for Vance's possible travel to the ceremony — a signing-logistics flight rather than a combat deployment. (Bloomberg, "Trump Says He'll Sign Deal With Iran to Reopen Hormuz Sunday"; CNBC; Fox News; Times of Israel; Just The News; NBC News; Axios, June 13, 2026.)

### New Wrinkles: "No Money Will Exchange Hands" and a Deferred "Go In and Get the Nuclear Dust" (June 13, 2026)

Trump introduced two departures from the long-reported 14-point MOU. First, cutting against Iran's stated precondition of a $24 billion frozen-assets release, he asserted "no money will exchange hands." Second, on the nuclear file he said the United States "will go in and get the Nuclear Dust, buried deep under the powerful sunken granite mountains" — to be down-blended and destroyed — but only at an undetermined later time "when all is calm." That restates, as a deferred post-deal step, the kind of in-country retrieval mission he had publicly rejected as a near-term option on June 5; it is not a ground-deployment order and carries no timeline. (Just The News; Times of Israel liveblog, June 13, 2026.)

An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Tehran had "not yet reached a final decision," and as of midweek Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's approval had not been obtained even though lower-ranking officials had approved the framework. The skepticism was underscored by the record: Trump had described a deal as imminent roughly 39 times across the talks, which had collapsed before despite such claims. (NBC News, "U.S.-Iran deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz could be signed within days, both sides say"; CNBC; Euronews, June 12-13, 2026.)

### Pakistan Reports a "Final, Agreed Upon Text"; Trump Floats a Weekend Signing in Europe — but the Deal Is Unsigned and Contested (June 12-13, 2026)

One day after Trump announced "a great settlement of the war with Iran," Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Islamabad's mediators believed a "final, agreed upon text" of an agreement to end the war had been reached and that they were working with both sides to finalize next steps, adding that peace "has never been this close as it is now." Senior US administration officials said Iran was holding "final" deliberations and that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei was "comfortable" with the negotiations, having committed that Iran would "never procure or develop nuclear weapons." Trump said a possible signing could come "maybe over the weekend in Europe," with Vice President JD Vance set to attend, and the UK was reported preparing to host a meeting of about 35 countries to coordinate reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Per Iran's Mehr news agency and US accounts, the reported 14-point MOU would reopen Hormuz immediately without tolls (pre-war volumes within 30 days), lift the US naval blockade and withdraw US forces from areas surrounding Iran, suspend US sanctions and release $24 billion in frozen Iranian funds, and commit Iran to the removal and destruction of its nuclear material and the dismantling of its program.

But the agreement was not signed, and the day laid bare a public dispute over its contents. In an angry Truth Social post, Trump said Iran had misrepresented the negotiations and that leaked details "have NOTHING to do" with the terms already agreed, calling the Iranians "very dishonorable people to deal with." Iran's Mehr countered that final negotiations would not begin until half of the $24 billion was released and the US naval blockade ended, and Netanyahu's office reiterated that Israel is not a party to the memorandum — leaving a live gap on sequencing even as Pakistan called the text "final." (RFE/RL, "Pakistani PM Says Final Text of US-Iran Peace Deal Has Been Reached"; The Hill; NBC News live blog; ms.now liveblog; CNBC, "Trump denies Iran's account of deal terms, decries new drone attack: 'Dishonorable people,'" June 12, 2026; House of Commons Library CBP-10636.)

### Fresh Iranian Drone Attack on Hormuz Shipping; Oil Falls to a Two-Month Low (June 11-12, 2026)

Even as the settlement was declared "final," the maritime conflict continued: overnight June 11-12 Iranian forces fired on Indian commercial shipping departing the Strait of Hormuz, and the US military shot down two Iranian attack drones near the strait early on June 12. Trump condemned the attack on the Indian ships as "totally unacceptable," saying it had been repelled; there were no US casualties, leaving the cumulative US KIA figure (15 total, 13 combat) unchanged. Markets nonetheless priced de-escalation: Brent crude extended its decline toward ~$88.40-$88.65/bbl in early trading — its lowest level in nearly two months — after settling near $90.38 (down ~2.9%) on June 11, and the US national pump average eased to about $4.11/gal. The structural floor (Hormuz still closed plus the dual blockade) remains intact; this is de-escalation pricing, not ground-commitment pricing. (CNBC; Yahoo/NBC News; TradingEconomics, Brent crude, June 11-12, 2026.)

### Apache Downing Triggers Two Nights of US Strikes — ~49 Tomahawks on June 10 (June 9-10, 2026)

The cycle began with the downing of a US AH-64 Apache helicopter over the Strait of Hormuz (~June 9); both pilots were reportedly rescued uninjured, and Washington blamed Tehran. The US struck Iran on two consecutive nights. On June 9 it bombed Qeshm Island and the ports of Sirik, Jask and Bandar Abbas, with Iran reporting destroyed water reservoirs and damaged telecommunications infrastructure. On June 10, CENTCOM ran a renewed four-hour campaign beginning ~22:15 GMT (completed ~9:04 p.m. ET) using, by Trump's account, about 49 Tomahawk cruise missiles against "military surveillance capabilities, communication systems, and air defense sites" across Iran — some targets as close as ~40 miles from Tehran — with locations including Karaj and Strait of Hormuz ports. Trump: "We were really close to a deal. But they keep tapping us along." The downing produced no US KIA, leaving the cumulative figure (15 total, 13 combat) unchanged. (Al Jazeera, "US bombs Iran after Trump threat, Tehran closes Hormuz Strait to all ships"; NBC News, "Iran strikes American bases after U.S. attacks over helicopter crash"; CNBC, June 10, 2026.)

### Iran Closes Hormuz "To All Ships" and Barrages US Bases in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan (June 10, 2026)

In response, Iran's IRGC declared the Strait of Hormuz "closed until further notice," warning that all traffic would be targeted — a hardening of the chokepoint beyond the existing dual blockade. Iran then launched drone and missile strikes on US forces at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa airbase (US Fifth Fleet), Kuwait's Ali Al Salem and Ahmad Al-Jaber airbases, and Jordan's Al-Azraq airbase (12 ballistic missiles); state media Tasnim claimed Iran "struck and destroyed eighteen important targets," and two oil tankers were reportedly hit. Bahrain's defenses intercepted the attack but an 11-year-old girl was injured and homes and vehicles damaged by debris; Jordan claimed interception of about 20 missiles with no casualties; southern Iran reported at least two wounded at Kargan. Kuwait closed its airspace at 4:50 a.m. local on June 11 as a precaution. (Al Jazeera, "Iran attacks Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan again after new waves of US strikes"; NBC News; CNBC, June 10-11, 2026.)

### Trump's Kharg-Seizure / "Total Control" Threat — the War's Most Explicit (June 11, 2026)

On Truth Social, Trump wrote: "At some point in the not too distant future, we will be taking Kharg Island, and other oil infrastructure points, and assume total control of their Oil and Gas Markets, much like we have with Venezuela." He separately posted that the US military would hit Iran "VERY HARD TONIGHT," and threatened to strike Iranian "power plants and bridges" if talks stalled, saying Iran would "have to pay the price." Kharg Island handles roughly 90% of Iran's crude exports. This was the first time the President publicly stated an intent to physically seize Iranian oil territory and assume "total control" of its oil and gas, explicitly invoking the Venezuela model — the strongest on-record articulation to date of a resource-seizure / occupation aim. (Euronews, "US will seize and control Iran's Kharg Island and other key oil facilities, Trump says"; CNBC; Axios; Times of Israel, June 11, 2026.)

### Same-Day Walk-Back, Cancelled Strikes, and a "Settlement" Announcement (June 11, 2026)

Within hours Trump reversed course. He told Fox News he was not sure "America has the stomach" to take Kharg, then cancelled the threatened Thursday-night strikes, saying discussions had been "brought to the highest level of Iranian leadership" and approved. He announced: "We just made a great settlement of the war with Iran, and we're going to be subject to finalization of documents, which should get done over the next few days," adding "Probably have a signing, maybe in Europe," and told the New York Post the agreement was "pretty much all wrapped up." He said he had sounded out the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Egypt, Turkey, Pakistan and others, all supportive. Reported terms track the long-negotiated 60-day MOU: Hormuz reopened with no tolls, Iran clears its mines, the US lifts its port blockade and issues sanctions waivers letting Iran sell oil freely, and nuclear negotiations follow. Two critical caveats: Iran did not confirm any deal, and Netanyahu said Israel is not a party to the emerging agreement. (NPR, "Trump now says a peace deal will be announced soon, cancels further strikes"; NBC News; Times of Israel, June 11 liveblog, June 11, 2026.)

The standing capability was unchanged — ~50,000 US troops in CENTCOM, three carrier strike groups, the USS Tripoli ARG / 31st MEU enforcing the blockade, the USS Boxer ARG / 11th MEU still under INDOPACOM, and the 82nd Airborne forward HQ (Maj Gen Tegtmeier) as a standing Kharg forcible-entry contingency rather than an execution order. ### Israel Strikes Iranian Territory for First Time Since April; Iran's 'Operation Nasr' Answers (June 8, 2026)
- Early **Monday June 8** Israel launched strikes on **central and western Iran** in response to Iran's June 7 missile fire — the **first Israeli strikes on Iranian soil since the April 8 ceasefire.** Iranian state television reported explosions in **Tehran, Isfahan, Karaj and Tabriz;** Iran's IRGC said Israel used **air-launched ballistic missiles.** Israeli strikes also hit a **petrochemical factory in the city of Mahshahr (Khuzestan province)** — later confirmed by the Israeli military — and the IDF said it targeted **truck-based surface-to-air missile launchers.** The overnight attacks were described as the **most serious escalation** since the April ceasefire.
- **Iran fired approximately 30 ballistic missiles in total since Sunday night,** launching a second wave after the Israeli strikes; the **IRGC branded the campaign "Operation Nasr" ("Victory")** and said it had targeted **two Israeli military bases.** Israel said it **downed the missiles;** most were intercepted, with **debris reaching Jordan and the West Bank.** **No casualties were confirmed from the missile exchange itself** — the only deaths in the cycle remain the June 7 Israeli strike on Beirut's southern suburbs (2 killed, ~20 wounded). (The Times of Israel, "Daily Briefing June 8 — Iran fires on Israel, reigniting smoldering war," June 8, 2026; Al Jazeera, "Iran and Israel bomb each other: Is the ceasefire over?", June 8, 2026; ABC News, "Israel and Iran trade strikes, threatening to drag region back to full-scale war," June 8, 2026.)

### Trump Blocks a Larger Israeli Strike — 'I Made Netanyahu Stop' (June 8, 2026)
- President **Trump intervened directly to stop a larger Israeli operation** against Iran that had been prepared for **late June 8 afternoon.** He said he **"made Netanyahu stop,"** that **"I call the shots,"** told the **Financial Times** that Netanyahu **"won't have any choice"** regarding a US-Iran agreement, and — per a US official — told Netanyahu by phone to refrain from further strikes because **"we are close to doing something good in terms of a deal."** Trump separately said he had **warned Netanyahu that Israel could be "left alone"** if it escalated the fight with Iran. This was the strongest single de-escalatory signal of the cycle and the clearest instance of the US acting as a **brake on its own ally.** (MS NOW liveblog, "Trump says he made Netanyahu stop Iran attacks," June 8, 2026; Arab News; The Times of Israel, June 8, 2026.)

### Both Sides Halt; Iran Attaches a Lebanon Condition; 'Immediate Ceasefire' Sought (June 8-9, 2026)
- **Iran's military command announced** that **"the cessation of armed forces operations is hereby announced"** after delivering what it called a **"painful response,"** and the **Iranian Foreign Ministry confirmed Iran had ceased its strikes** against Israel — but **warned that hostilities would resume if the IDF continues military operations in Lebanon.** **Israel halted its attacks** on Iran, with Netanyahu **confirming the halt while stopping short of acknowledging a ceasefire.**
- **Trump posted on Truth Social:** **"Both sides, Israel and Iran, are looking to do an immediate CEASEFIRE! ... Final negotiations on 'Peace' are proceeding, subject to ignorance or stupidity getting in its way."** The exchange — the **first direct, two-sided Israel-Iran territorial exchange since the April ceasefire** — thus ran its course in roughly 24 hours and **resolved toward de-escalation** rather than into sustained open war. (Arab News, "Trump says Israel and Iran 'looking to do an immediate ceasefire,'" June 8, 2026; CNN/CBS News live updates, June 8-9, 2026.)

### Oil Spikes Then Fades; OPEC+ Adds July Barrels; Talks Still Deadlocked Over $24B (June 8-9, 2026)
- **Brent crude crossed ~$98/bbl intraday Monday June 8** after the missile exchange, then **eased back to ~$94** once Iran announced it had ended operations against Israel; **WTI jumped more than 4% above $94.** Prices **faded on ceasefire optimism** and US-Tehran progress signals. **OPEC+ approved another increase in July production quotas of 188,000 bpd** despite persistent Middle East supply risks. **Hormuz** traffic stayed paralysed at roughly **36 transits/week** vs ~100-130/day before the war (analysts still estimate four to six months to normalize) — the price action remained **RISK/ESCALATION pricing, not the sustained $130+ that a ground commitment would imply.**
- Nuclear talks stayed **deadlocked over Iran's demand for $24 billion in frozen assets** ($12B on signing + $12B within 60 days). Reporting indicated Washington was **weighing redirecting some frozen Iranian assets to Gulf states** for reconstruction rather than front-loading relief to Tehran; IAEA inspector access remained limited; mediation continued via **Pakistan, Qatar, Turkey and Egypt.** (TradingEconomics, Brent crude, June 8-9, 2026; CNBC, "Oil eases as Iran ends operations against Israel," June 8, 2026; GlobalSecurity.org/RFE/RL, June 6, 2026.)

### Ground Rung — Unchanged Through the War's Most Extreme Escalation (June 8-9, 2026)
- **GROUND RUNG UNCHANGED — A VERTICAL ESCALATION THAT STAYED IN THE MISSILE/AIR REGISTER AND RESOLVED TOWARD DE-ESCALATION.** The June 8 exchange is the **highest-amplitude escalation of the war** — the first time since April that Israel struck Iranian territory and Iran struck Israeli territory in the same cycle — but it produced **no movement on the ground rung.** There were **no US ground troops in Iran, no Kharg Island ground assault, no third-ARG order, no new MEU order, no BCT-scale National Guard activation, and no Selective Service/draft action.** Decisively, the **US was not the kinetic actor** (the strikes were Israeli and Iranian; the US role was diplomatic restraint), and Trump's most consequential move was to **block a larger Israeli strike** — the opposite of a mobilization signal. Standing force unchanged: **~50,000 US troops** in CENTCOM; **three carrier strike groups** + the **USS Tripoli ARG / 31st MEU** (~2,200 Marines, ground-capable if ordered) enforcing the blockade; the **USS Boxer ARG / 11th MEU** remains under INDOPACOM. On the draft, only the pre-existing administrative plan for **automatic Selective Service registration by end-2026** persists — no activation, no enabling legislation; fact-checkers (PolitiFact, Poynter) continue to rate a draft unlikely. (Breaking Defense, Apr 2026; CNBC, Apr 9, 2026; PolitiFact, Mar 9, 2026.)

### Beirut Tripwire Crossed — Israel Strikes Beirut, Iran Fires First Direct Missile Barrage at Israel Since April Ceasefire (June 7, 2026)
- On **Sunday June 7** Israeli warplanes **struck Beirut's southern suburbs (Dahieh)** without warning, in what Netanyahu's office called retaliation for **Hezbollah firing at northern Israel;** Israel said it targeted Hezbollah **"command centers."** Lebanon's Health Ministry said the strike **killed two and wounded about 20, including four women and four children.** The strike came **despite a US request** days earlier that Israel stand down on Beirut.
- **Iran responded the same day with its first direct missile barrage on Israel since the April 8 ceasefire** — directly actualizing FM **Abbas Araghchi's June 4 warning** that "any attack on Beirut" would trigger a **"full-scale resumption"** of the war. Iran's state broadcaster confirmed the launches; the Israeli military said its **Iron Dome and Arrow** systems were activated and intercepted missiles but that **"the defense is not hermetic,"** with air-raid sirens across several areas of northern Israel and multiple explosions.
- **Casualty reporting diverged.** The IDF's initial statement said **no immediate casualties or damage** were reported; subsequent reporting (**NPR**) described an Iranian missile with a **cluster warhead** striking a building in **Ramat Gan and killing two residents in their 70s,** with debris from the barrage falling on the **Old City of Jerusalem** and causing damage near the **Al-Aqsa Mosque/Temple Mount, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the Jewish Quarter.** (NPR, "Israel says Iran launched a missile at it, in a first during fragile ceasefire," June 7, 2026; PBS NewsHour, "Israel says Iran launched missiles in first bombardment since fragile ceasefire," June 7, 2026; Axios, "Iran fires missiles at Israel for first time since ceasefire," June 7, 2026; CSMonitor; The Washington Times, June 7, 2026.)

### Official Reactions — IRGC Threat, Israeli Vow, Iran's 'Ceasefire Violation' Charge (June 7-8, 2026)
- **Iran's Revolutionary Guard** declared that **"should these acts of aggression be repeated, the responses will be broader in scope and will encompass all American and Zionist targets throughout the region,"** and Iranian lawmaker **Ebrahim Rezaei** (parliament national-security committee) vowed a **"decisive and painful response."**
- **Iran's Foreign Ministry** framed the **June 6 US strikes on Iranian radar sites at Goruk and on Qeshm Island** as **"a clear violation of the 8 April ceasefire and an act of military aggression,"** explicitly putting the US — not only Israel — in the frame.
- On the Israeli side, IDF spokesman **Brig. Gen. Effie Defrin** said **"Iran has made a grave mistake,"** and chief of staff **Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir** vowed to **"strike the enemy with determination as soon as the order is given."** (CBS News live updates, "Iran retaliates after Israel's deadly strike in Beirut, accuses US of violating ceasefire as peace talks stall," June 7-8, 2026; PBS NewsHour; Al Jazeera, June 7, 2026.)

### Trump Pushes De-escalation; Distances US From the Beirut Strike (June 7-8, 2026)
- President **Trump** moved to contain the escalation. He told Israel's **Kan** broadcaster he did **not think Israel needed to respond further** to Iran's barrage, and said Israel's Beirut strikes were **"not coordinated with the US and I'm not happy about it."** He told **Fox News:** "What I would suggest to Iran: You've shot your missiles, that's enough… Get back to the table and make a deal," and told **Axios** he would **call Netanyahu to urge him not to retaliate.**
- Accounts of pre-notification diverged: some reporting said Israel **notified the administration before the strike** and that the US **"supports Israel's right to self-defense,"** while Trump publicly described it as uncoordinated. Trump also downplayed the oil shock, noting Brent was near ~$97 rather than the "$300" a full Hormuz cutoff might imply. (Axios, "Israel strikes Beirut after Hezbollah attack, risking Iran response," June 7, 2026; CBS News live updates, June 7-8, 2026; Al Jazeera, June 7, 2026.)

### Second Kinetic Flare-Up — Iran Strikes Kuwait and Bahrain; US Downs Drones and Missiles (June 6, 2026)
- **U.S. Central Command** said its forces **shot down four Iranian one-way attack drones** launched toward the Strait of Hormuz, describing them as **"an immediate threat to regional maritime traffic,"** and **intercepted six of seven Iranian ballistic missiles fired at Kuwait and Bahrain** — the seventh failed to reach its target. **Bahrain's Defense Ministry** said its air defenses **intercepted and destroyed three missiles and a number of drones,** air-raid sirens sounded across the island, and it accused Iran of continuing to attack the country with "missiles and drones targeting civilians." This was the **first time Bahrain was directly targeted** in the war (the June 3 barrage hit Kuwait only), widening the conflict to a **second Gulf host of US forces.**
- In response, US forces **struck Iranian coastal surveillance radar sites in the city of Goruk and on Qeshm Island** "to defend against further attacks." CENTCOM said Iran uses those sites to overlook the maritime routes near Hormuz and track vessels entering the Persian Gulf, and that they host naval assets, drone infrastructure and anti-ship missile systems; CENTCOM added that **"American forces remain vigilant and postured to respond to unjustified Iranian aggression in self-defense."** **Iran's Mehr news agency** characterized the drone launches as **"warning shots"** fired near the strait, most likely linked to the movement of US ships around the waterway. No new casualties were reported from the June 6 intercepts. (CENTCOM, "CENTCOM Forces Defeat Missiles, Drones Launched by Iran," June 6, 2026; Fox News live updates, "US strikes Iran radar sites after drones near Hormuz, missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain," June 6, 2026; Middle East Monitor, June 6, 2026; RFE/RL, "US Forces Hit Iranian Coastal Sites After Tehran Launches Drones Toward Strait," June 6, 2026; ABC7; India TV News, June 6, 2026.)

### Trump: Iran's Nuclear Ambitions 'Finished'; Tehran at '21-22%' of Its Missile Arsenal (June 6, 2026)
- President **Trump** said Iran's nuclear ambitions are **"finished"** and estimated that Tehran now has only **"21%-22% of its missile arsenal compared to what it had before"** the US strikes in February. A White House official said Trump **"isn't going to rush into a bad deal"** and would not allow Iran to possess nuclear weapons. The remarks accompanied the June 6 kinetic exchange and underscored the administration's framing that pressure — not front-loaded concession — will set the terms of any agreement. (Fox News live updates, June 6, 2026; The Statesman, "Hormuz flashpoint: US downs Iranian drones, strikes radar sites; Trump says Tehran's nuclear ambitions finished," June 6, 2026.)

### Talks Still Deadlocked Over $24B; US Sanctions Iranian LNG/LPG Networks (June 6, 2026)
- Negotiations remained stalled over Iran's demand for the immediate release of **$24 billion in frozen assets** ($12 billion on signing of an interim agreement and a further $12 billion later), which adviser **Mohsen Rezaei** framed June 5 as a **"test of trust."** Washington refused to front-load the relief and instead imposed **fresh sanctions on Iranian liquefied-petroleum-gas and oil-smuggling networks.** **IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi** continued to say talks may be inching toward a preliminary nuclear framework, with the open obstacles being restored inspector access and verification of Iran's **~60% enriched-uranium stockpile** (options: export, dilution, or IAEA custody). (Fox News live updates, June 6, 2026; The Soufan Center, "U.S.-Iran Distrust Holds Up an Agreement," June 1, 2026; CNN; The Express Tribune, June 5, 2026.)

### Kuwait Expels Two Iranian Embassy Staff Over the June 3 Attack (June 5-6, 2026)
- **Kuwait demanded that two Iranian embassy staff leave** the country following the **June 3** drone-and-missile barrage that damaged the passenger terminal at **Kuwait International Airport,** killed one Indian national and wounded 63. Kuwait said the June 3 attack had targeted civilian and vital facilities, **"including diplomatic missions."** The expulsion marks a hardening of Gulf-state diplomatic posture toward Tehran even as Kuwait and Bahrain again came under fire June 6. (Gulf News, "Kuwait demands two Iran embassy staff leave after deadly attack," June 2026; NPR/PBS, "Kuwait says Iranian drones hit airport and killed 1," June 3, 2026.)

### Lebanon — Israeli Strikes Kill Three Lebanese Army Officers (June 6, 2026)
- **Israeli airstrikes in southern Lebanon on June 6 killed nine people, including three Lebanese Armed Forces officers** — a notable escalation of the fraying **June 4 conditional ceasefire framework,** which Hezbollah's **Naim Qassem** had already rejected as an "imaginary ceasefire" amounting to "surrender." Striking **uniformed LAF personnel** — rather than Hezbollah fighters — risks drawing the Lebanese state directly into the conflict and complicates the US-brokered framework that envisions the LAF policing "pilot" zones south of the Litani. The Lebanese Health Ministry's cumulative toll stands at roughly **3,500 killed** since March 2. This remains **US-brokered diplomacy plus Israeli operations in Lebanon — not US ground troops in Iran.** (Fox News live updates, June 6, 2026; CNN, "Israel-Lebanon ceasefire frays as Iran warns of wider war," June 5, 2026; Al Jazeera, June 5-6, 2026.)

### Oil, Hormuz, and the Ground Rung (June 6-7, 2026)
- **Oil** eased to about **$94.81/bbl on June 6** (down from ~$95.25 on June 5), holding well above the pre-war $60-70 band but far below the sustained $130+ that a ground commitment would imply — **risk/escalation pricing, not ground-commitment pricing,** despite the day's kinetic flare-up and the geographic widening to Bahrain. Reduced Chinese crude imports (softer demand) also weighed on prices. **Hormuz** traffic stayed paralysed at roughly **36 transits in the prior seven days** versus ~100-130 cargo vessels per day before the war; analysts still estimate **four to six months** to normalize. (Fortune, "Current price of oil as of June 5/June 6, 2026"; TradingEconomics, June 6, 2026.)
- **GROUND RUNG UNCHANGED — HORIZONTAL, NOT VERTICAL, ESCALATION.** The June 6 exchange is the cycle's **second kinetic flare-up** (after June 2-3) and its **first geographic widening to a second Gulf state,** but it remained entirely within the **air/naval + missile/drone register:** Iran fired drones and ballistic missiles, the US answered with intercepts and a **proportional radar-site strike** at Goruk/Qeshm — **not a ground deployment.** None of the tracked vertical indicators moved: **no US ground troops in Iran, no Kharg Island ground assault, no third-ARG order, no new MEU order, no BCT-scale National Guard activation, and no Selective Service/draft action.** The widening to Bahrain is **horizontal escalation** (more targets in the same register), not a vertical move up the ladder toward a ground commitment. USS Boxer ARG remained under **INDOPACOM;** USS Gerald R. Ford home at Norfolk; USS Abraham Lincoln + USS George H.W. Bush CSGs + USS Tripoli ARG in the Arabian Sea enforcing the blockade. (CENTCOM; GlobalSecurity.org; Fox News, June 6, 2026.)

### Other Theatres — Russia-Ukraine / DPRK / US-China / Latin America (June 3-7, 2026)
- **Russia-Ukraine:** The front remained largely static. ### Rezaei: Talks 'At a Deadlock' Over $24 Billion; Warns of a Wider War (June 5, 2026)
- In an exclusive CNN interview in Tehran, **Mohsen Rezaei** — military adviser to Supreme Leader **Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei** — said **"the negotiations are at a deadlock and Trump must break this deadlock,"** adding **"the ball is in Trump's court."** A potential interim agreement now hinges on the US releasing **$24 billion in frozen Iranian assets — $12 billion upon signing and a further $12 billion at a later stage** — which Rezaei cast as **"a test of trust that Iran wants to have with Trump … this is a test that America must pass and the path will be opened,"** stressing it is Iranian money, not American funds. He warned Iran would **"drag the war"** beyond the Persian Gulf and **"give another dimension to the war by attacking these other American bases"** if fighting resumed, and said **"our land power is many times greater than our missiles."** He proposed that **Iran and Oman jointly manage the Strait of Hormuz** and charge **"maintenance fees"** rather than tolls, and characterized the conflict as Iran's **"first triumph"** in its 47-year history. US officials are concerned that unfreezing the funds at this stage would remove a key leverage point and resemble handing over **"pallets of cash."** (CNN, "Exclusive: Iran supreme leader's adviser says talks deadlocked over $24 billion and warns of wider war," June 5, 2026; Newsmax; The Express Tribune; The Times of Israel liveblog, June 5, 2026.)

### Trump Reveals — and Rejects — a US-Ground 'Nuclear Dust' Recovery Plan (June 5, 2026)
- President Trump disclosed that he had **considered but rejected** a risky operation to **send US troops into Iran to physically collect enriched uranium,** saying the mission would have required **"at least two weeks"** on the ground and the airlift of **"massive equipment."** He decided against it, describing the nuclear material as **"entombed"** and saying there was **"no reason to"** proceed. This is the most explicit US-ground-operation deliberation surfaced in the war to date — and it **resolved against deploying ground forces,** with the administration continuing to favor recovery/destruction of HEU via negotiated IAEA mechanisms. (ABC News / ABC7 live updates, "Iran live updates: Trump details risky, rejected plan to collect 'nuclear dust,'" June 5, 2026.)

### IAEA: Possible Movement Toward a Preliminary Nuclear Framework (June 5, 2026)
- **IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi** indicated negotiations may be progressing toward a preliminary nuclear framework while cautioning that outcomes remain uncertain. He named the key obstacles as restoring consistent **inspector access** and verifying Iran's **~60% enriched-uranium stockpile,** and said several technical options exist — **export, dilution, or IAEA custody** — but each requires a political decision. Separately, the **US announced fresh sanctions** targeting Iranian oil-smuggling networks, specifically **LPG smuggling to South and East Asia** and illicit financial transactions moving billions of dollars in oil-derived funds. (RFE/RL; ABC News live updates, June 5, 2026.)

### Lebanon — Aoun Blames Iran; Hezbollah Calls It an 'Imaginary Ceasefire'; Fresh Strikes (June 5, 2026)
- Lebanese President **Joseph Aoun** accused Iran of **"using Lebanon as a bargaining chip"** in its negotiations with the US even as Israeli strikes continued under the **June 4 conditional ceasefire framework.** Hezbollah Secretary-General **Naim Qassem** said the terms of the **"imaginary ceasefire"** would amount to a **"surrender"** — requiring Hezbollah to stop fighting and withdraw south of the Litani while Israel **"continues its aggression."** Lebanon's National News Agency reported **four people killed Friday** in Israeli strikes on **Nabatieh and Bint Jbeil;** the IDF ordered the forced displacement of residents in **at least nine** southern towns and villages and said it killed **Abed Harb,** commander of Hezbollah's engineering unit responsible for assembling explosives used against IDF soldiers. **France requested an emergency UN Security Council session** on Lebanon. The Lebanese Health Ministry's toll stands at roughly **3,500 killed** since March 2 with nearly a fifth of the population displaced. This is **US-brokered diplomacy plus an Israeli ground operation in Lebanon — not US ground troops in Iran.** (Al Jazeera, "Iran war live: Lebanon's president criticises Iran amid Israeli attacks," June 5, 2026; CNN, "Israel-Lebanon ceasefire frays as Iran warns of wider war," June 5, 2026; The Times of Israel liveblog, June 5, 2026; UN News, June 2026.)

### Oil, Hormuz, and the Ground Rung (June 5-6, 2026)
- **Oil** held the mid-$90s — Brent about **$95.25/bbl on June 5 (+0.23%),** with an intraday print near **$97.44** at the NY open — well above the pre-war $60-70 and far below the sustained $130+ that ground-commitment pricing would require; the structural floor (Hormuz closure + US blockade) remained intact and the pricing stayed **risk/escalation, not ground-commitment.** **Hormuz** traffic stayed paralysed: only about **seven vessels transited the strait Friday with four more departures over the weekend (~36 in the seven days to Friday)** versus ~100-130 cargo vessels per day before the war; analysts estimate **four to six months** to normalize once a deal lands. (Fortune, "Current price of oil as of June 5, 2026"; Gulf News; World Oil; Bloomberg, June 2026.)
- **GROUND RUNG UNCHANGED, TILTING DEESCALATORY.** The defining ground-rung development was **Trump's on-record rejection of a US-troops-into-Iran uranium-recovery mission** — the clearest US ground-option deliberation of the war, resolved against deployment. **Rezaei's** threat of a "wider war" and attacks on US bases, plus his **"land power"** boast, is Iranian retaliatory/defensive rhetoric in a **missile/base register,** not a US ground trigger. There were **no new US ground-troop deployments, no third ARG order, no new MEU order, no BCT-scale National Guard activation and no Selective Service/draft action;** USS Boxer ARG remained under **INDOPACOM,** USS Gerald R. Ford home at Norfolk, and USS Abraham Lincoln + USS George H.W. Bush CSGs + USS Tripoli ARG in the Arabian Sea enforcing the blockade. The House's June 3 war-powers resolution (215-208) remained the dominant counter-escalatory domestic signal. (CENTCOM; GlobalSecurity.org; ABC News; CNN, June 5-6, 2026.)

- **Russia-Ukraine:** FM **Sergei Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow's insistence on the April 2022 Istanbul draft** as the basis for any settlement — a document treating Russia as a "guarantor state" with veto power over responses to future aggression and imposing strict neutrality and force limits on Ukraine.
