## 14. North Korea

### September 7 Update — An Eighteenth Day Without a Launch, and Seoul's Hormuz Options Still Contain No Ground Element (September 6, 2026)

**No external action.** **No nuclear test, no ICBM or satellite launch, no inter-Korean military incident, no DMZ event and no new statement from Kim Jong Un** were reported through the cutoff. The US and South Korean push for talks has produced no reported movement.

**Internal consolidation remains the standing picture.** The revised DPRK constitution, released in full by **Seoul's Ministry of Unification** on **May 6, 2026**, institutionalises Kim Jong Un's expanding absolute authority and elevates the office of **State Affairs Commission Chairman** above the constitutionally designated supreme organ of state power. **Kim Yo Jong** became director of the **Workers' Party General Affairs Department** in **February 2026**. Elections to the **15th Supreme People's Assembly** were held **March 15, 2026**.

**The strategic assessment is unchanged.** The **2026 Annual Threat Assessment** records the DPRK as committed to expanding its strategic weapons programmes and investing in nuclear-capable systems to deter the United States, challenge regional missile defences and hold targets in South Korea at risk. Kim has rejected denuclearisation negotiations since 2019.

**The Korean development that bears on the Iran theatre is South Korean, and it is unchanged.** Seoul's **September 4** statement stands: its review of options for a Hormuz contribution **remains in progress** and **no decision has been made**. The options reported — a **maritime patrol aircraft**, a **logistics support vessel** and a **mine detection and clearance unit** — **contain no ground element.**

**Sources:** 38 North, “Consolidating Kim's Rule,” July 2026; Republic of Korea Ministry of Unification release of the revised DPRK constitution, May 6, 2026; US Intelligence Community 2026 Annual Threat Assessment; Congressional Research Service IF10472; South Korean government statement on Hormuz deployment options, September 4, 2026.

### September 5 Update — A Sixteenth Day Without a Launch, and Seoul Publicly Walks Back the Hormuz Deployment (September 4, 2026)

**The retraction.** The South Korean government publicly pushed back on reports that concrete preparations were under way to send military forces to the **Strait of Hormuz**, stating that a **review of options — including military measures — remains in progress and no decision has been made.** **This briefing logged the deployment on September 4 as the first new allied military contribution to the Hormuz theatre and moves it back to untested.**

**And the options described today are smaller than the ones described yesterday.** The reported candidates are a **maritime patrol aircraft**, a **logistics support vessel**, and a **mine detection and clearance unit**. Yesterday's reporting centred on the **Cheonghae Unit** — the **4,400-tonne destroyer *Wang Geon***, about **260 personnel** including a **naval special warfare boarding team** and **Lynx helicopters**, which sailed from **Jinhae on May 15, 2026** and is presently restricted to waters off **Somalia**. **Every option now named is surveillance, sustainment or mine countermeasures. None is a combatant contribution and none puts Korean personnel on another state's deck or soil.** Several South Korean outlets had reported that Seoul aimed to dispatch **before the end of the year** and could seek **National Assembly approval this month**; expanding the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations requires **both a government decision and parliamentary approval**.

**The pressure is American and documented.** President **Trump** publicly criticised South Korea last month for what he characterised as a **direct refusal** to assist American efforts in the Strait, making the remarks alongside his order **abruptly curtailing a large-scale joint US-ROK military exercise**. **The sequence matters for the alliance ledger: an American president reduced a joint exercise with a treaty ally, in public, as leverage to obtain a naval contribution to a different theatre — and the ally has so far produced a review rather than a ship.**

**Pyongyang did nothing.** The last launch remains roughly **ten short-range ballistic missiles** fired from Pyongyang on **August 20** during US-ROK exercises — the **ninth ballistic launch of 2026**, following launches on January 4, March 14, April 19, June 25 and August 12 among others. **Sixteen consecutive days without a launch as of September 4.** No nuclear test, no NLL or DMZ incident. The *Just Security* Early Edition for September 4 carried **no Korea item at all**.

**The diplomatic datum is unchanged.** On **August 18** Trump said **Kim Jong Un** had responded to his request for a conversation and described the exchange as **“very positive,”** without detail; **no meeting has been announced** eighteen days later. President **Lee Jae-myung** continues to state a commitment to normalising relations with the North.

**Korean exposure to the Hormuz war continues.** The **Sinokor-operated *Senegal Prosperity***, a Korean-operated hull carrying two million barrels of Saudi crude, was struck off **Khasab** on **August 31**.

**Sources:** The Japan Times, “South Korea reviewing military options for Hormuz, no decision made, official says,” September 4, 2026; UPI, “Seoul says no decision yet on Hormuz military deployment,” September 4, 2026; Reuters via Yahoo News Canada, “South Korea prepares Hormuz military deployment, media reports say,” September 3, 2026; The Korea Times, “Navy to deploy 4,400-ton destroyer to Cheonghae unit amid ongoing Iran war,” May 15, 2026; Militarnyi, “North Korea Conducts Ninth Ballistic Missile Launch of 2026,” August 2026; Just Security, “Early Edition: September 4, 2026”; Al Jazeera, “Trump says N Korea's Kim has responded to his request for a conversation,” August 18, 2026.

### September 4 Update — A Fifteenth Day Without a Launch, and Seoul Prepares to Send Warships to the Persian Gulf (September 3, 2026)

**Pyongyang.** No launch. The last event remains approximately **ten or more short-range ballistic missiles** fired from **Pyongyang** at about **5 p.m. KST on August 20, 2026** — the third ballistic test of that month — timed against large-scale **US-ROK joint exercises** and against Chinese Foreign Minister **Wang Yi's** meeting with President **Lee Jae Myung** in Seoul; Japan's defence ministry issued a coast guard alert at **5:08 p.m.** warning vessels in the area. Nothing since. The **Ninth Congress of the Workers' Party (February 19-25, 2026)** set a five-year line emphasising further nuclear and missile development, conventional upgrades and **naval operational capability**; fifteen days of quiet does not alter it.

**The peninsula's real movement was South Korean, and it points at the Gulf.** Reporting this cycle says **South Korea is preparing a military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz** in support of freedom of navigation, aiming to dispatch **before the end of the year**. The candidate formation is the **Cheonghae Unit**, Seoul's standing anti-piracy detachment — currently **Cheonghae Unit 48**, built around the **4,400-tonne destroyer *Wang Geon***, which sailed from **Jinhae on May 15, 2026** on a six-month rotation, the ninth overseas deployment of that hull. The contingent numbers around **260 personnel**, including the ship's company, a **boarding team from the naval special warfare flotilla** and an aviation element flying **Lynx helicopters**. Its authorised area of operations is presently confined to **waters off Somalia**; extending it to Hormuz requires both a **government decision and National Assembly approval**.

**Why it matters to this briefing.** South Korea is among the two **most Hormuz-dependent major economies** in the world, and one of its own operated hulls — the Sinokor-operated **Senegal Prosperity** — was struck **17 nautical miles east of Khasab on August 31** carrying two million barrels of Saudi crude. **A Korean deployment would be the first new national military contribution to the Hormuz theatre by a US ally reported in this war, and it would arrive with a special-warfare boarding capability at precisely the moment CENTCOM has begun boarding vessels for “total compliance.” It is a naval and constabulary commitment, not a ground one: an ally drawn toward the chokepoint by its own energy exposure, through its parliament, on a six-month rotation.**

**No inter-Korean incident, no Northern Limit Line event, no announced change to US-ROK exercise posture, and no DPRK response to the prospective Korean Gulf deployment.**

**Sources:** *The Times of Israel* live blog, September 3, 2026; *Reuters* via Yahoo News Canada, “South Korea prepares Hormuz military deployment, media reports say,” September 3, 2026; *The Korea Times*, “Navy to deploy 4,400-ton destroyer to Cheonghae unit amid ongoing Iran war,” May 15, 2026; *The Korea Herald*, “Can South Korea afford to deploy naval forces to the Strait of Hormuz?”; Seoul Economic Daily, “Korea's Cheonghae Unit 48 Sets Sail Amid Possible Hormuz Deployment,” May 15, 2026; NK News, “North Korea launches barrage of short-range missiles from Pyongyang,” August 20, 2026; Japan Ministry of Defense, “Recent Missile & Nuclear Development of North Korea.”

### September 3 Update — A Fourteenth Day Without a Launch, and the Pacific's Carrier Gap Becomes Indefinite Rather Than Temporary (September 2, 2026)

**The launch record.** No DPRK launch since the approximately **ten KN-25 short-range ballistic missiles** of **August 20** — **fourteen consecutive days**. That barrage remains **unpublicised in North Korean domestic media**, the signature of a test conducted for external audiences rather than internal ones.

**The degradation this cycle is American and it deepened.** The **USS George Washington (CVN-73)** with **Carrier Air Wing 5** — the forward-deployed carrier based in Japan — is operating in the **Arabian Sea** in support of Operation Epic Fury. **What is new this cycle is that the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) is preparing to relieve her there.** That converts a temporary absence into a standing commitment: **the Pacific's dedicated carrier coverage is not returning when George Washington's rotation ends, because her relief is going to the Gulf too.** The **USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72)**, which George Washington relieved, **docked in Thailand this cycle after 286 days at sea**.

**The standing concessions are unchanged and entirely one-sided.** THAAD has left the Korean peninsula. The forward-deployed carrier is in another theatre. INDOPACOM commander **Adm. Samuel Paparo** filed one of the four formal four-star **non-concurs** recorded in the **August 14 Secretary of Defense Orders Book** against the stripping of his theatre to sustain the Iran campaign, and **that non-concur stands unanswered**. **Pyongyang has not had to do anything to obtain any of it.**

**Seoul's posture is unchanged.** President **Lee Jae Myung** continues to press domestic military modernisation — artificial intelligence, drones, and the potential acquisition of a **nuclear-powered submarine** — **the response of a government planning for reduced American coverage rather than expecting its restoration**. Kim Jong Un's standing position from the **February 2026** party congress is unaltered: expansion of the nuclear arsenal, permanent exclusion of South Korea from the category of compatriots, and no dealings with Seoul. **No launch, no test, no statement and no negotiation this cycle.**

*Sources: American Enterprise Institute, “China & Taiwan Update, September 1, 2026”; Just Security, “Early Edition: September 2, 2026”; Daily NK current coverage, September 2026; Republic of Korea Joint Chiefs of Staff — no launch announcement, September 2, 2026.*

### September 2 Update — A Thirteenth Day Without a Launch, and the American Position on the Peninsula Degrades Further Without Pyongyang Doing Anything (September 1, 2026)

**The launch record.** No DPRK launch since the approximately **ten KN-25 short-range ballistic missiles** fired from the Pyongyang area on **August 20** as the shortened **Ulchi Freedom Shield** neared its end — **thirteen consecutive days**. That barrage has **still not been publicised in North Korean domestic media**, a sustained choice not to claim it at home.

**The concession ledger, unchanged and still unreciprocated.** **THAAD** interceptors redeployed **from South Korea** to the Middle East. The **USS George Washington** repositioned from **Japan** to the **Persian Gulf**, leaving the Pacific without carrier coverage. **INDOPACOM commander Adm. Samuel Paparo** filing a formal non-concur against the continued demand for his carrier strike group and destroyers. **Ulchi Freedom Shield** ordered *"substantially reduced"* by the President hours before it began, running **five days instead of eleven** with its **counteroffensive phase never conducted**, and a further exercise cancelled since. The President tied his displeasure to **Seoul's refusal to join US action against Iran**. Pyongyang has returned nothing.

**The cycle's new datum is American and bureaucratic.** On **August 31**, **Army Secretary Dan Driscoll** resigned effective **September 3**, and Hegseth had already asked the **Army chief of staff** to step down. The United States Army — the service that mans the roughly **28,500**-strong US contingent in Korea and would generate any reinforcement of it — now has **neither a Senate-confirmed civilian secretary nor a Senate-confirmed military chief**. That is not a Korean event, but it is a Korean fact.

**Seoul's position.** President **Lee Jae-myung** has said South Korea must brace for a **"worst-case scenario,"** maintains the exercises are defensive, and his office has expressed hope that the *"friendly"* Kim-Trump relationship *"will lead to meaningful US-North Korea dialogue."* Trump has said he expects to meet Kim again this year; **nothing is scheduled** and Pyongyang has not responded.

**What Pyongyang is doing instead is selling.** Zelensky's weekly accounting of Russian expenditure against Ukraine — nearly **2,000 strike drones**, more than **1,600 aerial bombs** and **31 missiles** — **included North Korean ballistic missiles**. The DPRK's munitions are being consumed in Europe while its deterrence problem in Asia is being solved for it in Washington.

*Sources: The Washington Post, "Military leaders warn Hegseth against extending Iran war operations," August 30, 2026 (August 14 Secretary of Defense Orders Book); Bloomberg and Military Times on the Driscoll resignation, August 31, 2026; Wall Street Journal via Just Security, "Early Edition: September 1, 2026"; Reuters via US News & World Report, "North Korea Launches 10 Ballistic Missiles as US-South Korea Drills Near End," August 20, 2026; CBS News, August 20, 2026; CNBC, "South Korea must brace for worst-case scenario, President Lee says," August 18, 2026; Breitbart, August 21, 2026; Euronews, August 30, 2026.*


### August 25 Update — The Exercise Ended Early and Its Counteroffensive Phase Never Took Place (August 21-24, 2026)

**The concession was larger than this briefing first recorded, and the correction is entered.** **Ulchi Freedom Shield**, the annual US-South Korean command-post exercise, was originally scheduled as an **eleven-day event in two phases**: **defensive operations through Friday August 21**, then **counteroffensive operations through August 27**. It was curtailed to **five days** as a goodwill gesture, and South Korea's military confirmed it **ended on Friday August 21**. **The second phase — the counteroffensive half, which is the half Pyongyang denounces most loudly as an invasion rehearsal — did not take place at all.** The concession was therefore not the shortening of a single exercise but the **deletion of its offensive component**.

**The sequence, assembled.** On **August 18-19** the exercise reduction was announced and President Trump confirmed he expects to meet **Kim Jong Un** this year — *"Yeah, I will be,"* and of Kim, *"I get along with him great"* — putting Pyongyang's arsenal at **"57 very powerful nuclear weapons."** On **August 19** **Kim Yo Jong** dismissed the reduction, saying it does not change the drills' **"provocative, aggressive nature,"** and **denied** that Kim Jong Un had responded to any request from Trump for a conversation. On **August 20** North Korea fired **about ten KN-25 short-range ballistic missiles** from the Pyongyang area roughly **185 miles (~300 km)** toward the sea. On **August 21** the drills ended.

**Since then, silence.** North Korea has issued **no comment on its own launches**, a departure from its usual practice of publicising tests. **No further launch has been reported. No date and no venue for a Trump-Kim meeting has been announced.** The **August 12** and early-August short-range launches remain the preceding pattern.

**The state of the theatre is a concession made, refused in words, answered in ordnance, and then quietly completed anyway** — with the offering side having given up the exercise phase it originally intended to run and received nothing on the record in return.

*Sources: The Korea Times, "S. Korea, US wrap up drills early, day after NK missile barrage," August 22, 2026; PBS News/AP, "U.S.-South Korea military drill wraps up early, a day after North Korea's missile barrage," August 21, 2026; U.S. News/AP, August 21, 2026; The Korea Times, "N. Korea remains silent over latest missile launches," August 21, 2026; CBS News, "North Korea launches ballistic missiles as Trump seeks to rekindle nuclear talks with Kim Jong Un," August 20, 2026; Eastern Herald, "North Korea Fires 10 Missiles After Trump Curtails Ulchi Freedom Shield, Announces Kim Summit," August 22, 2026.*

### August 24 Update — Backfill: A Presidential Summit Offer Sat Between the Concession and the Barrage, and Was Refused With It (August 19-20, 2026)

**This briefing had recorded the exercise reduction and the missile barrage but not the summit offer that sat between them, and the omission changed the shape of the sequence.** On **August 19**, speaking to reporters outside the White House, President **Trump** was asked whether he expected to meet **Kim Jong Un** this year and answered **"Yeah, I will be,"** saying of the North Korean leader **"I get along with him great"** and putting Pyongyang's arsenal at **"57 very powerful nuclear weapons."** A summit would be his **fourth meeting with Kim** and his **first since returning to office**; **no date or venue was given**.

**The concession was also larger than recorded.** **Ulchi Freedom Shield** began on **August 17** and had been scheduled to run to **August 27**. It was **curtailed from eleven days to five** as a goodwill gesture toward Pyongyang, on top of the **August 18** announcement by Seoul and Washington that they would scale back the drills.

**The answer was the third ballistic event of the month.** On **August 20**, around **5 p.m.**, North Korea fired a barrage of **about ten short-range ballistic missiles** from the capital region, which South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said flew **roughly 300 kilometres** toward the **East Sea**. The system is the **600mm KN-25**, which Pyongyang has previously described as capable of delivering **tactical nuclear warheads**. The launches follow events on **August 6** and **August 12**. **Kim Yo Jong** had dismissed the drill reduction on **August 19**, saying the exercises' **"provocative, aggressive nature"** would not change with reduced duration and size, and has **denied that any Trump-Kim contact has taken place**. Seoul convened an **emergency security meeting**. The package refused was therefore not a curtailed exercise alone but a curtailed exercise **plus a presidential summit offer**, refused inside 48 hours.

**The Russian track continues.** ISW reports **North Korean drone operators deployed to Kursk oblast** — a move up the capability ladder from the infantry deployments of earlier phases, and the reason the 2026 Ulchi Freedom Shield scenario was reshaped around lessons from the DPRK's Russian experience.

*Sources: NBC News, "Trump says he will meet with Kim Jong Un this year," August 19, 2026; The Washington Post, August 19, 2026; US News/Reuters, August 19, 2026; Korea JoongAng Daily, August 2026; Al Jazeera, "North Korea fires ballistic missiles as US-South Korea drills end," August 20, 2026; Stars and Stripes, August 13 and August 20, 2026; Eastern Herald, August 22, 2026; Institute for the Study of War, August 21, 2026.*

### August 23 Update — A Scaled-Back Exercise Announcement Is Answered With Ten Missiles Inside 48 Hours (August 17-21, 2026)

**The sequence is the diagnostic fact, not the launch.** On **August 17** the annual **Ulchi Freedom Shield** exercise began. On **August 18** Seoul and Washington announced they would **reduce the duration and scale** of their joint drills, an explicit signal aimed at reopening diplomacy. On **August 19** Pyongyang shrugged the gesture off, with **Kim Yo Jong** — the influential sister of Kim Jong Un — saying the drills' **"provocative, aggressive nature"** would not change even with their reduced duration and size. On **August 20**, around **5 p.m.**, North Korea fired a barrage of **about ten short-range ballistic missiles** from the **capital region** toward the sea. The concession was made, refused in words, and answered in ordnance within 48 hours.

**It is the third ballistic event of the month.** North Korea fired a short-range ballistic missile from the **Wonsan area on August 6**, its first ballistic activity since late June, and what appeared to be a **midrange ballistic missile** toward the sea east of the peninsula on **August 12**. The August 20 barrage takes the year's tally to **eleven suspected ballistic events**. President Trump had described Kim Jong Un as **"well behaved"** shortly before the launches and has sought to rekindle nuclear talks.

**And the peninsula is now materially connected to the European war in a new way.** ISW's **August 21** assessment reports that **North Korea has deployed drone operators to Kursk Oblast** in support of Russia, assessing that the deployment will let North Korean forces acquire tactical and technological skills critical to contemporary warfare. Pyongyang's earlier contributions were manpower and shells; drone crews return home with transferable expertise.

**No nuclear test, no ICBM, no satellite launch and no attack** accompanied any of the August activity.

*Sources: U.S. News & World Report / AP, "North Korea Fires Barrage of Missiles Toward the Sea After Dismissing Overture From Trump," August 20, 2026; Al Jazeera, "North Korea fires ballistic missiles as US-South Korea drills near end," August 20, 2026; NPR, August 20, 2026; CBS News, "North Korea launches ballistic missiles as Trump seeks to rekindle nuclear talks with Kim Jong Un"; The Diplomat, August 2026; Institute for the Study of War, August 21, 2026.*

### August 22 Update — The 157-Day Provocation Pause Ends With Ballistic Launches on August 6 and August 12 (August 2026)

**Two launches, and a correction to this briefing's prior framing.** Through **August 2** this record noted 157 consecutive days without a new DPRK provocation. That run ended. On **August 6** North Korea fired a **short-range ballistic missile**, its **first ballistic testing activity since late June**, and on **August 12** it launched again, the projectile flying **more than 700 kilometres** before falling into the sea — **Pyongyang's eleventh suspected ballistic test of 2026** — as **South Korea and the United States** prepared announced military drills. Neither launch produced casualties, an inter-Korean incident or a nuclear test.

**The production track is the more consequential one.** **Kim Jong Un**'s order at a missile industrial facility in early June for a **2.5-fold increase in ballistic and cruise missile production** stands. ## 15. Trump Third Term

### Legislative Attempts
- **January 23, 2025**: Rep. Andrew Ogles (R-TN) introduced **H.J.Res.29** proposing a constitutional amendment allowing election to the presidency up to three times (but not three consecutive terms -- designed to exclude Obama/Bush/Clinton while enabling Trump).
- Supported by conservative groups like the "Third Term Project" at CPAC 2025.

### Trump's Own Statements
- **March 30, 2025**: Trump told NBC News "there are methods" for seeking a third term and said he was "not joking."
- Suggested one method: VP Vance wins a future election and "hands over" the presidency. Refused to elaborate on other plans.
- **May 2025**: Walked it back on Meet the Press, saying "it's not something I'm looking to do" and he plans to "have four great years and turn it over to somebody, ideally a great Republican."

### Constitutional Reality
- Amending the Constitution requires two-thirds of Congress or a constitutional convention (34 states), plus ratification by three-fourths of states. This remains an extremely high bar.
- No serious legislative progress on the amendment as of March 2026.

## 16. Venezuela — Operation Absolute Resolve and Aftermath

### September 7 Update — No New Development; the Maduro Calendar and the American Concession Both Stand (September 6, 2026)

**No new development was reported through the cutoff.** **Delcy Rodríguez** remains **acting president**, having been sworn in after the **January 2026** US operation that captured **Nicolás Maduro** and **Cilia Flores** and transported them to New York.

**The case.** Both stand charged with **narcoterrorism conspiracy**, **conspiracy to import cocaine into the United States**, **possession of machine guns and destructive devices**, and **conspiracy to possess those weapons**. **Trial is set for June 1, 2027.** The defence's deadline to submit arguments for dismissal fell on **September 2, 2026**; **no ruling has been reported.**

**The concession.** The **August 28** grant of a **100-year concession** over fields holding **65 billion barrels** to a joint venture in which the **United States government holds 55%** stands unamended. **No US-China grand bargain over Venezuelan oil exists**, and the prediction that one would materialise was scored **disconfirmed** in the September 1 pass.

**The ground-relevant negative.** **No US ground operation was reported in Venezuela this cycle.** The January operation remains the only American ground action of 2026 in the hemisphere, and it was a **short-duration seizure, not an occupation**.

**Sources:** ABC News and NBC News reporting on the June 1, 2027 trial date; GlobalSecurity, “U.S. court sets June 2027 trial for Venezuelan President Maduro amid protests,” July 23, 2026; Wikipedia, “2026 United States intervention in Venezuela,” as of September 6, 2026.

### September 5 Update — The Oil That Justified the Intervention Will Not Arrive This Decade, and the Maduro Case Acquires Its Full Calendar (September 4, 2026)

**The economic premise was priced, and it is measured in decades.** *The National* reports that the roughly **$100 billion** American bet on Venezuelan crude will deliver far more slowly than advertised. Most of the reserves are **extra-heavy** and require expensive upgrading facilities: as one analyst put it, **“It's almost like solid. You can almost compare it with the tar sands in Canada.”** **Kpler's** crude analysis lead: **“These are huge types of equipment that you just cannot build in a couple of years.”** The forecasts carried: approximately **1.4 million bpd by 2028**; additions of **at most 300,000 bpd by 2030**; a return to **three million bpd only by 2040**; greenfield projects producing nothing **until about 2033 or 2034**; and a realistic ceiling of **1.2-1.3 million bpd** rather than a theoretical 1.5 million. **Against that, Energy Secretary Chris Wright projected two million bpd by the end of the decade.** US-bound Venezuelan exports have already risen **238% to average 515,000 bpd** in early 2026.

**The commercial commitments, and the question of authority.** **North American Blue Energy Partners** plans investment across **17 projects**. **Chevron** has committed more than **$7 billion over five years**, more than doubling its production to about **600,000 bpd**, with additional **Orinoco Belt** acreage; **Eni** and **GE Vernova** signed alongside in the eight energy agreements executed in Caracas in the presence of Energy Secretary **Chris Wright**. Under the deal, **$19 from every barrel** produced and sold to the US flows to Caracas — an arrangement described as potentially worth **$209 billion per year** to Venezuela. **Energy analysts have questioned whether acting President Delcy Rodríguez has the legal authority to grant 100-year rights over 17 fields holding 65 billion barrels; Trump says the agreement lasts a century and Rodríguez says twenty-five years.** *Foreign Policy* asked this cycle whether the deal will hinder Venezuelan democratisation.

**The Maduro prosecution now has a full calendar.** Prosecutors must respond to the **head-of-state immunity** motions by **October 2**. Judge **Alvin K. Hellerstein** will hear the dismissal effort on **November 17**. **Trial remains set for June 1, 2027.** **Maduro**, held in a **Brooklyn federal jail**, has pleaded not guilty; counsel **Barry Pollack** argues that customary international law confers **status-based head-of-state immunity** and that the acts alleged would have been part of his official duties, and that the court therefore lacks jurisdiction. **Cilia Flores** claims spousal protection. **The United States ceased recognising Maduro as Venezuela's legitimate president in 2019 and rejected his claim of victory in the 2024 election, which is the principal argument against the immunity claim.**

**What this means for the tracked predictions.** Predictions that American control of Venezuelan oil would **rapidly reshape global supply** move toward **disconfirmed** on a specific and dated mechanism: the binding constraint is **upgrader construction**, the analyst consensus places meaningful new volume in the **2030s**, and the official 2030 projection is contradicted by the commercial trackers. **The theatre that was supposed to offset Hormuz cannot do so on any timescale relevant to this war.** Predictions that the capture would be **judicially reviewed in the United States** are **confirmed**; predictions that Maduro would be **tried and convicted** remain **untested**.

**Elsewhere in the hemisphere this cycle.** **US Southern Command** intercepted and sank a vessel it said was refuelling drug-trafficking operations by the **Los Choneros** organisation. **Haiti's** foreign minister urged the **UN Security Council** to renew the international force's mandate ahead of **December elections**, as more than **100 people** were deported to Haiti on a third consecutive Thursday flight. In the South Atlantic, Argentine President **Milei** escalated his dispute with Britain over the **Falkland Islands** with tougher sanctions targeting companies involved in a major offshore oil project; the UK reaffirmed the islanders' right of self-determination.

**Sources:** The National, “US $100bn Venezuela oil bet faces years-long wait,” September 4, 2026; Foreign Policy, “Will the U.S.-Venezuela Oil Deal Hinder Democratization?,” September 4, 2026; Reuters and JURIST on the Maduro and Flores immunity motions and the October 2 / November 17 schedule, September 2-4, 2026; Al Jazeera, “Venezuela's Maduro asserts immunity in US court, urges dismissal of charges,” September 3, 2026; UPI, “U.S. firms gain majority control of 65B oil barrels in Venezuela,” September 2, 2026; NPR and The Washington Times on Chevron's $7bn expansion, September 2, 2026; Al Jazeera, “US's Chevron, Italy's Eni to expand oil projects in Venezuela,” September 3, 2026; Just Security, “Early Edition: September 4, 2026.”

### September 4 Update — Maduro Moves to Dismiss on Head-of-State Immunity, Putting the Legality of the January Capture Before a US Judge for the First Time (September 2-3, 2026)

**The motions.** **Nicolás Maduro** and **Cilia Flores** filed **separate motions** in Manhattan federal court on **Wednesday September 2** seeking dismissal of the narco-terrorism indictment. Maduro's counsel **Barry Pollack** argued the court **lacks jurisdiction** on two grounds: that **sovereign heads of state enjoy complete immunity** from prosecution, and that the acts alleged **would have been part of his official duties**. The pleading's load-bearing claim is that Maduro **remained Venezuela's head of state for immunity purposes notwithstanding the United States' refusal to recognise him** as the country's legitimate president. **Flores** contends she is protected as the **spouse of a sitting head of state**. Judge **Alvin Hellerstein** will hear the motions on **November 17**; trial remains scheduled for **June 1, 2027**. The charges are four counts including **narco-terrorism conspiracy** and **cocaine importation conspiracy**, carrying a maximum of life imprisonment.

**Why it reaches beyond the defendant.** If head-of-state immunity attached at the time of the acts and at the time of the seizure, then the **January 2026 US military operation** that removed Maduro and Flores from Venezuela and delivered them to an American court was **the abduction of a serving head of state**. **The motion therefore puts the legality of the operation, not merely the sufficiency of the charges, before a US district judge for the first time**, and the government's answer will be the first on-the-record American legal justification for the capture.

**The successor government is so far unaffected.** Acting President **Delcy Rodríguez** — sworn in **January 5, 2026**, the first woman to exercise the Venezuelan presidency — has restructured the armed forces, met a series of Washington's demands, and had her own US sanctions lifted in **April**. **621 political prisoners** were confirmed released as of March 8, with **500+** remaining per **Foro Penal**. The **August 28 hundred-year concession** over fields holding **65 billion barrels**, to a joint venture in which the **United States government holds 55%**, stands.

**Sources:** *Reuters* via CP24, BusinessWorld and West Hawaii Today, “Venezuela's Maduro asserts immunity, urges US judge to dismiss charges,” September 3, 2026; JURIST, “Former Venezuelan President Maduro and wife move to dismiss drug trafficking indictment on sovereign immunity grounds,” September 3, 2026; *The Washington Times*, September 2, 2026; POLITICO via Just Security, September 3, 2026; CNN Politics, “Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro gets a June trial date,” July 22, 2026.

### September 3 Update — The Control Terms Are Published and They Go Further Than the Equity: A US Government Veto Over Board Appointments and a Mandated American Majority of Directors (September 2, 2026)

**The governance terms are new and they are the story.** The White House and Caracas released the full terms of the **North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP)** arrangement. Beyond the **Defense Department's 35% equity stake** and the **State Department's guaranteed right to purchase 20% of output at the cost of production** with a right of first refusal on the remainder: **the United States government holds veto authority over NABEP board appointments, and a majority of the company's directors must be American citizens.** **Equity of 35% does not confer control; a veto over board appointments plus a mandated American majority on the board does.** The operative fact about this transaction is not the Pentagon's minority stake but that **Washington determines who governs the company holding a century of rights over roughly 21% of Venezuela's proven reserves**.

**The structure and the numbers.** NABEP is headquartered in **Barbados** with offices in Venezuela, is controlled by Venezuelan businessman **Alejandro Betancourt**, holds **100-year concessions over 17 fields** and **retains operating control**. It seeks to finance **up to $100 billion** in investment to rehabilitate and expand production. Acting President **Delcy Rodríguez** said the first phase could generate approximately **$209 billion for Venezuela** and that roughly **$19 from every barrel** would flow to the Venezuelan government. The 17 fields could eventually produce **more than 1.5 million bpd**. President Trump said **Exxon is going in**.

**China protested, formally and by name — and did nothing else.** Foreign ministry spokesman **Guo Jiakun**: *“China's legitimate rights and interests in Venezuela must be guaranteed.”* **Five of the 17 fields** were joint ventures with Chinese companies including state-owned **CNPC** and Hong Kong-registered **China Concord Petroleum**. US Energy Secretary **Chris Wright** told Bloomberg that **China will not have claims to Venezuelan oil revenue**. **Beijing's response to the expropriation of its position in a country where it was the principal creditor is a foreign ministry statement.**

**The industry objection is on the record.** Oil executives and advisers quoted in the reporting question whether companies can compete on equal terms against an operator backed by a **US government shareholder**, **century-long concessions** and **guaranteed government purchasing rights**. Paul Krugman publicly attacked the concession.

**Maduro.** The defence deadline to file its motion to dismiss fell on **September 2, 2026**; counsel **Barry Pollack** is arguing **head-of-state immunity**. Judge **Alvin Hellerstein** has set trial for **June 1, 2027** in the Southern District of New York on narcotics-trafficking and weapons charges to which Maduro and **Cilia Flores** pleaded not guilty.

*Sources: NBC News, “Days after Trump announces Venezuela oil deal, White House fills in some of the details,” September 2, 2026; FDD's Long War Journal, “White House, Caracas release details on historic US-Venezuela oil deal,” September 2, 2026; PR Newswire, “United States Government and North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) Reach Historic Deal to Develop Venezuela's Oil Sector,” September 2026; South China Morning Post, “China demands rights guarantee as US firm secures 100-year Venezuelan oil deal,” September 2, 2026; Bloomberg, “China Won't Have Claim to Venezuela Oil Revenue, Wright Says,” September 2, 2026; Caracas Chronicles, “Trump's Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Gusher of Controversy,” September 2, 2026; CNN, “Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro gets a June trial date,” July 22, 2026.*

### September 2 Update — The White House Names the Counterparty and Publishes the Structure, Which Corrects This Briefing's "55%" Figure (September 1, 2026)

**The counterparty has a name and an owner.** The White House said the Venezuela arrangement will run through **North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP)**, owned by Venezuelan businessman **Alejandro Betancourt**, already the **second-largest operator in Venezuela behind Chevron**. Acting President **Delcy Rodríguez** is granting NABEP **100-year rights over 17 oil fields** with **proven reserves of 65 billion barrels**.

**The US government's position is two instruments, not one.** The **United States Defense Department** will be granted a **35% stake** in a private company created as a joint venture with NABEP. The **State Department** will then have the right to buy **20% of NABEP's output at the cost of production**, and a **right of first refusal** to buy everything else.

**This briefing carried "55%" and corrects it here.** Since **August 28** the record has read that the concession went to *"a joint venture in which the United States government holds 55%."* The September 1 disclosure **decomposes that number into a 35% Pentagon equity stake and a 20% State Department offtake right at cost — two categorically different things**. Equity is ownership; an offtake right at production cost is a purchase option. **The corrected record: DoD 35% equity in the JV; State 20% of output at production cost plus first refusal on the remainder.** The 65-billion-barrel reserve figure and the 100-year term are confirmed, and the number of fields is now specified at **17**.

**Why the Pentagon line matters.** The department taking equity in a foreign oil venture is the **Defense Department**. This briefing records that without editorialising and notes only that it is unusual in the American institutional record. Reuters reports that the fields being transferred were **previously operated by Chinese and Russian firms**, which makes the transaction a **displacement of Beijing and Moscow from Venezuelan production** as well as a commercial arrangement. **Rodríguez** has described the deal as a chance to modernise Venezuela's oil industry and accelerate its revival while insisting sovereignty remains secure; analysts quoted in the same reporting expect **legal challenges and questions of legitimacy**. **Chevron is separately expanding** its Venezuelan operations as the administration pushes US majors back in.

**Standing items, no change.** **Maduro's** federal trial before Judge **Alvin Hellerstein** remains set for **June 1, 2027**. The **August 14 Secretary of Defense Orders Book** records **SOUTHCOM** among four commands filing formal non-concurs, stating that continued diversion of ships and surveillance aircraft to CENTCOM has **degraded its ability to meet homeland-defence obligations**. **A sixth consecutive cycle with no new security event in the region.**

## 17. Cuba — Cascading Crisis

### September 7 Update — No New Development; the Fuel and Electricity Crisis Is Unrelieved (September 6, 2026)

**No new development was reported through the cutoff.** The cascading crisis is **unchanged in kind and unrelieved in degree**.

**The mechanism.** Fuel shortages have gripped the island since the **January 2026** capture of Nicolás Maduro removed Cuba's principal oil supplier. The **executive order of January 29, 2026** established a mechanism for **additional tariffs on goods from any country that directly or indirectly supplies oil to Cuba**; the threat has made even willing suppliers cautious and reduced **tanker arrivals to nearly zero**.

**The state of the grid.** Cuba reported having **no fuel, no oil and no diesel** as of **May 14, 2026**. Following the **July 6** nationwide blackout, only about a **third of Havana's electricity** had been restored by **July 7**, with controlled outages elsewhere stretching to **thirty hours**.

**The standing figure.** The Cuban government's count of **32 members of its military and intelligence services killed** during the US intervention in Venezuela stands.

**Sources:** CNN, “Cuba hit with nationwide blackout as US pressure continues,” July 6, 2026; Axios, “Cuba's humanitarian crisis worsens as U.S. talks stall,” May 28, 2026; Executive Order of January 29, 2026; CounterPunch, “Cuba after Six Months of the Oil Blockade,” August 14, 2026.

### September 5 Update — The State Department Sanctions the Island's Last Two Hard-Currency Earners (September 4, 2026)

**The designations.** The **US State Department** imposed sanctions on **five Cuban companies** and a **grandson of Raúl Castro**, citing family connections and involvement in the **nickel mining** and **energy** sectors. **Those are the two remaining hard-currency earners on an island whose energy ministry says all fuel reserves are exhausted.**

**The conditions the sanctions land on.** Some areas are taking **blackouts of 20 to 22 hours per day**. Cuba recorded its **sixth nationwide grid failure of 2026** in **August**, with storms disrupting restoration less than a day after the collapse. **Only one oil tanker — Russian — has been permitted to dock since January**, when the intervention in Venezuela severed the supply that had sustained the grid; oil imports fell effectively to **zero in January 2026**, the first time since **2015**, after Mexico also suspended planned exports. Nearly **one million Cubans** depend on tanker trucks for drinking water, and **84% of pumping equipment requires electricity** — when the grid goes down, so does the water supply.

**The one external advocate.** **Colombia's Petro** has been among the few regional leaders publicly defending the island, urging Washington to change course, saying Cuba **“should be helped and applauded,”** and ordering a shipment of Colombian rice in **May 2026** for which **Díaz-Canel** publicly expressed thanks. Petro made what was described as his **final official visit** to Havana as president in **August 2026**.

**Prediction status.** Corpus predictions of a **Cuban state collapse** remain **untested-trending**: exhausted reserves, 20-22 hour blackouts, one permitted tanker since January, a sixth nationwide grid failure — and a government still standing, now subject to fresh designations aimed at its nickel and energy earnings.

**Sources:** Just Security, “Early Edition: September 4, 2026”; Al Jazeera and Caribbean National Weekly on Cuba's fuel and grid crisis, 2026; CNN, “Storms disrupt Cuba's power restoration, operator says, less than a day after sixth nationwide blackout,” August 3, 2026; Think Global Health, “Cuba's Health Care Buckles Under Fuel Blockade”; CiberCuba on Petro's August 2026 visit.

### September 4 Update — The Energy Ministry Declares the Reserves Exhausted, with 20-22 Hour Daily Blackouts (September 2026)

**The state's own account.** Cuba's **energy and mines ministry** says **all fuel reserves are now exhausted**, and that as a result some areas are experiencing **electricity blackouts of 20 to 22 hours per day** — the most severe figures logged in this theatre. Supplies of **diesel and fuel oil have virtually run out**. The island has recorded its **eighth nationwide outage since late 2024** and its **third of 2026**.

**The structural cause is an American policy instrument, and it is quantified.** Under the de facto US oil blockade, **since January the United States has permitted exactly one oil tanker — from Russia — to dock in Cuba**, according to Cuban authorities. Compounding it is a grid whose infrastructure largely dates from **1960-1980**.

**The consequences.** Transport, hospitals, water supply, industry and public services are all disrupted; shortages of **food, drinking water and medicine** are deepening across a population of **9.6 million**. **The government has not fallen.**

**Sources:** Al Jazeera, “Cuba suffers second island-wide blackout in a week amid Trump fuel blockade”; Caribbean National Weekly, “Cuba suffers third nationwide blackout of 2026 amid worsening fuel crisis”; Think Global Health, “Cuba's Health Care Buckles Under Fuel Blockade”; Wikipedia, “2024-2026 Cuba blackouts” (aggregating the above).

### September 3 Update — Service Fails for a Full Twenty-Four Hours as the School Year Opens, and the Structural Cause Is an American Policy Instrument (September 2, 2026)

**The forecast became the failure.** Cuba's state utility **UNE** had forecast a peak-hour shortfall of up to **2,310 MW** for September 1. **Electricity service was compromised for a full 24 hours on Monday** on generation shortfall, **with outages persisting into Tuesday**. The **2026-2027 school year opened under those conditions**.

**The structural cause is worth restating because it is an American policy instrument.** **Since January the United States has allowed only one oil tanker — from Russia — to dock in Cuba.** Cuba's electricity system has deteriorated amid shortages of fuel and replacement parts and repeated breakdowns at ageing thermoelectric plants; generation has been **unable to meet half of national demand since late 2024**.

**The standing record.** **Six nationwide grid collapses in 2026**, most recent **August 2-3**; scheduled blackouts above **18-20 hours a day**, with some areas of Havana exceeding **24 hours** and some rural communities exceeding **70 hours**. **A utility that publishes a numbered shortfall forecast and a government that opens the school year on schedule through a 24-hour service failure is a state administering a catastrophe, not a state ending.**

*Sources: CubaHeadlines, “Cuba Faces New School Year Amid Severe Power Outages: Forecasts Predict Blackouts of Up to 2,310 MW,” September 2026; CNN, “Storms disrupt Cuba's power restoration, operator says, less than a day after sixth nationwide blackout,” August 3, 2026.*

### September 2 Update — The Utility Publishes a Numbered Shortfall Forecast and the School Year Opens Anyway (September 1, 2026)

**No new grid event, and a forecast instead of a failure.** Cuba's state utility **UNE** forecast that during **peak hours on September 1** the national grid could face a shortfall of **up to 2,310 MW**, following a day whose peak shortfall reached **2,323 MW**. The **2026-2027 school year opened under those conditions**.

**The standing record is unchanged and is worse than the event count suggests.** **Six nationwide grid collapses in 2026** — twice in March, three times within ten days in July, and once on **August 2-3**, when thunderstorms disrupted restoration less than a day after the sixth collapse. Scheduled blackouts run **above eighteen to twenty hours a day**, with parts of Havana beyond twenty-four hours and some rural areas beyond thirty. Generation has been unable to meet **half of national demand** since late 2024. Fuel shortages tied to US sanctions remain the proximate driver.

**The analytical point, restated.** A utility that publishes a **numbered shortfall forecast** and a government that **opens the school year on schedule** constitute a state **administering a catastrophe**, not a state ending. This briefing continues to record **Cuban state collapse as disconfirmed** and the distinction between grid failure and state failure as the reason.

*Sources: Cubaheadlines, "Cuba Faces New School Year Amid Severe Power Outages: Forecasts Predict Blackouts of Up to 2,310 MW," September 2026; CNN, "Storms disrupt Cuba's power restoration, operator says, less than a day after sixth nationwide blackout," August 3, 2026; Al Jazeera, "Cuba's power grid collapses again despite restoration efforts," August 3, 2026.*


### August 25 Update — No New Grid Event; the Cumulative Figures Are Consolidated and They Are Worse Than the Event Count Suggests (August 24-25, 2026)

**No new nationwide failure was reported this cycle, and the running totals are consolidated here.** Cuba's national electricity system has now collapsed **six times in 2026** — **twice in March**, **three times within ten days in July**, and **once on August 2-3**. Reporting describes **blackouts exceeding twenty hours a day**, with some communities recorded at **up to 105 consecutive days without steady electricity**. The event count understates the condition: the island is not experiencing intermittent failures against a working baseline, it is experiencing a baseline of near-total outage punctuated by total collapse.

**The proximate cause remains fuel and the fuel cause remains policy.** Cuba lost its principal supplier when Washington imposed an **oil blockade** on the island following the **January 3** seizure of **Nicolás Maduro**, and imports from **Mexico have also been halted** amid US pressure. Sanctions run under **Executive Order 14404**; **Visa and Mastercard processing has been lost**; and the **United Nations** has described a **humanitarian emergency endangering lives**. Industrial output and transport remain crippled.

**Havana reports no movement.** Foreign Minister **Bruno Rodríguez** said last week that there had been **"no progress"** toward ending the impasse.

**The structural point this briefing records:** the instrument being applied to Cuba is the same instrument now formally applied to Iran — an oil blockade plus a sanctions order, pursued to the point of state-level economic failure, without the deployment of ground forces.

*Sources: Al Jazeera, "Cuba's power grid collapses again despite restoration efforts," August 3, 2026; Al Jazeera, "Cuba suffers second island-wide blackout in a week amid Trump fuel blockade," July 10, 2026; CBS News, "Cuba slowly getting power back after third nationwide blackout in 6 months: 'This is agony'"; PBS NewsHour, "Cuba reports island-wide blackout as country struggles with energy crisis"; compilation "2024-2026 Cuba blackouts."*

### August 23 Update — No New Grid Event; the Island Is Still Recovering (August 21-22, 2026)

**No new nationwide failure was reported this cycle.** Cuba is still recovering from the **sixth nationwide blackout of 2026**, when the national electricity system collapsed late on **Sunday August 2**, leaving roughly **ten million people** without power, and **thunderstorms disrupted the restoration effort** the following day by taking generating units offline again during the reconnection of the National Electric System. The run of collapses dates from the Trump administration's effective severing of Cuba from its main oil source in **January**. Havana residents have been sleeping on the **Malecón** to escape the heat during outages.

*Sources: CNN, "Storms disrupt Cuba's power restoration, operator says, less than a day after sixth nationwide blackout," August 3, 2026; Al Jazeera, "Cuba's power grid collapses again despite restoration efforts," August 3, 2026; PBS NewsHour, August 2026.*

### August 22 Update — Sixth Nationwide Blackout of the Year, Then Nine More Companies Sanctioned (August 2-20, 2026)

**The grid failed again.** Cuba's national electricity grid **collapsed late on Sunday August 2**, the island's **sixth nationwide blackout of 2026**, plunging about **ten million people** into darkness; **thunderstorms disrupted the restoration effort** the following day, with the grid operator reporting setbacks less than a day after the collapse. The grid had already failed **three times in nine days in July**.

**The cause remains fuel.** Cuba has lost its principal supplier as **Venezuelan** crude and product deliveries fall away under US pressure, and **imports from Mexico have ceased**. The system has deteriorated amid shortages of fuel and replacement parts and repeated breakdowns at ageing thermoelectric plants. The Energy and Mines Ministry's earlier statement that **all fuel reserves are exhausted** stands, with blackouts of **20-22 hours a day** in some areas.

**Washington tightened further.** On **August 20** the US Treasury and State Department imposed **new sanctions on nine Cuban state-owned companies and the leadership of the Cuban Institute**, targeting the **mining and construction** sectors.

*Sources: CNN, "Storms disrupt Cuba's power restoration, operator says, less than a day after sixth nationwide blackout," August 3, 2026; Al Jazeera, "Cuba's power grid collapses again despite restoration efforts," August 3, 2026; NBC News; AP News via Just Security Early Edition, August 21, 2026.*


### July 29 Update — A Fourth Island-Wide Blackout of 2026 and a Diplomatic Rupture With Incoming Colombia (July 2026)
Cuba has now suffered its **fourth island-wide blackout of 2026**, leaving about **10 million people without power**, under the combination of the halted Venezuelan crude supply following Maduro's January capture and **Executive Order 14380 of January 29**, which authorises tariffs on any country directly or indirectly supplying Cuba with fuel. The blocked shipments had covered about **60% of the roughly 100,000 barrels a day** the island's power system requires; generating capacity has fallen below demand with plants breaking down faster than they can be repaired. Diplomatically, **Cuba's foreign ministry publicly rejected Colombian president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella's announcement that he will close Colombia's embassy in Havana and sever bilateral ties**; he also plans to close the embassy in Managua and to restore relations with the United States and Israel. The handover in Bogotá is **August 7**.

### September 7 Update — No New Development (September 6, 2026)

**No new development was reported in Colombia through the cutoff.** The economic emergency and the US pressure campaign continue as previously recorded, and **no US ground operation in Colombia was reported this cycle.**

### September 4 Update — A UN Fact-Finding Mission Places Up to 2,000 Colombian Contractors on the RSF's Drone Systems in Sudan (September 3, 2026)

**The finding.** A **United Nations fact-finding mission** reported that foreign weapons, technology and fighters are sustaining the Sudanese civil war, and named a supply network involving the **UAE, Chad, Libya and Somalia** furnishing the **Rapid Support Forces**. The mission stated that **up to 2,000 Colombian contractors** helped **operate drone systems** for the RSF.

**The responses.** The **UAE rejected** the allegations; **Somalia** said it took them seriously; **Colombia** said it **opposes mercenarism**.

**Why it is logged here.** The finding places Colombian nationals in the **drone-operator** role — not perimeter security — in an African civil war to which Bogotá is not a party, and it does so in a week when Colombian-American security relations are already strained. **No Colombian state involvement is alleged, and no prosecution has been announced.**

## 19. Hormuz-Dependent Economies and the Widening Energy-Infrastructure War

### September 7 Update — Washington Publishes a Throughput Figure That Does Not Reconcile With Its Own Transit Count, and Iran Draws a Zone Over the Lanes These Economies Use (September 6, 2026)

**Three figures, three sources, one waterway — and this briefing states all three rather than choosing among them.** US Energy Secretary **Chris Wright** put flows through the Strait at approximately **9 million barrels per day**, roughly **two-thirds of pre-conflict levels** once **pipeline substitution** is counted. Iran's **Mohsen Rezaei** described the Strait as **“completely closed,”** with only **seven to eight ships** passing. The **straits.live** board carried **six transits** against an **85/day pre-crisis baseline** — 7% of normal — with the Strait recorded as **closed to commercial shipping**. **The American figure and the transit counts are not measuring the same object:** Wright's includes volumes routed through the Saudi **East-West pipeline** and the UAE's **Fujairah** terminal that **bypass the Strait entirely**, while the transit counts measure **hulls**. This briefing carries the **transit count** as its metric of record and logs the disagreement in the open-questions register rather than resolving it.

**The exposure structure is unchanged and is why the dispute matters.** Around **80%** of crude and oil products shipped through Hormuz and nearly **90%** of the LNG is **Asia-bound**. **East Asia absorbs 80-84% of the direct impact.**

**South Asia remains the most acutely exposed.** **Qatar and the UAE account for 99% of Pakistan's LNG imports, 72% of Bangladesh's and 53% of India's.** Pakistan and Bangladesh have **limited storage and limited procurement flexibility** and are the least able to substitute. **India faces an LPG supply crisis** attributable to the conflict.

**Northeast Asia is better stocked and worse priced.** **Japan holds 254 days** and **South Korea 208 days** of strategic petroleum reserves, and both have been **releasing from the joint stockpile** to moderate prices. Their exposure is to **spot-market volatility rather than physical shortage**, and it has landed on their equity markets: the **Kospi is down 12%** and the **Nikkei 225 down 8.6%**.

**Iran's announced restricted zone is a new variable for every one of these economies.** A zone **beginning at the line of the US Navy's blockade** and **extending into the Gulf**, policed by an **Iranian sanctions list**, would nominally apply to the **Japanese, Korean, Indian and European charterers** whose cargoes originate inside it. **No operator response had been published through the cutoff.**

**The governing commercial fact is unchanged.** **Mitsui O.S.K. Lines** — the world's largest tanker operator — **withdrew its resumption timeline on September 4** and will not return without **guarantees of sustainably safe passage**. **War-risk insurance stands at 40.0× pre-crisis, about $10.0 million per VLCC passage (+3,900% versus peacetime).**

**Gulf producers, unchanged.** The IMF's April 2026 revisions put 2026 contractions at **Qatar -14.7%, Kuwait -4.2%, Bahrain -3.8%, UAE -1.9%, Saudi Arabia -1.4% and Oman -0.05%**. Iran's **March 2026** attack on the **Ras Laffan** LNG facility eliminated an estimated **17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity** — about **3% of global supply** — with losses expected to persist for years. **Energy exports from Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain remain effectively halted.**

**Sources:** Iran International live blog, September 5-6, 2026 (Wright, Rezaei); NBC News/Associated Press, September 6, 2026; Gulf International Forum, “Hormuz Disruptions and Asia's Energy Resilience”; Zero Carbon Analytics, “Asian countries most at risk from oil and gas supply disruptions in Strait of Hormuz”; CNBC, “Strait of Hormuz closure: which countries will be hit the most,” March 3, 2026; Beyond the Horizon, “The Economic Clock of War”; World At Net, “Japan & India Face a New Energy Shock,” September 2026; Congressional Research Service R48971; Stimson Center, “Iran Conflict Hits Foundations of Gulf Economies”; IMF Regional Economic Outlook revisions, April 2026; straits.live board, 06 September 2026 2257Z.

### September 5 Update — The World's Largest Tanker Operator Says It Is Not Coming Back This Year, and a European Central Bank Moves Its Gold (September 4, 2026)

**The operator withdrew its timeline.** **Mitsui O.S.K. Lines** — the world's largest tanker operator — expects Hormuz disruption to last longer than it had assumed. CEO **Jotaro Tamura**: **“Given the current situation, it's difficult to see operations resuming in any form by the end of the year.”** MOL had previously assumed a **phased resumption from October** followed by a **return to normal operations from January**; that timeline now slips. **MOL does not currently plan to return to shipping oil through the Strait and says it needs guarantees and evidence of sustainably safe passage before it would consider the route again.** **This is a commercial judgement rather than a political forecast, made by the party that bears the hull risk, and it is more pessimistic than the prediction markets: the straits.live board gives reopening by December 31 a 27% probability, down from 28%.** Before the war, roughly **25% of the world's seaborne oil trade** and **20% of global LNG** passed through the Strait.

**And a central bank moved its gold out of North America.** **De Nederlandsche Bank** disclosed that between **March and August** it transferred approximately **86 tonnes of gold** — more than a quarter of the bullion it held in **New York** and **Ottawa**, worth roughly **$10-12 billion** — to **London**, citing **increasing geopolitical unrest** and **crisis preparedness**. More than **27 tonnes** were physically moved from the US and Canada to **Zeist** and an equivalent quantity from Zeist to London, avoiding melting; the remainder was executed by buying and selling. The **London share of Dutch reserves rose from 18.1% to 32.1%**; **30.8%** remains in the Netherlands. DNB President **Olaf Sleijpen**: **“We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness.”** **The stated reason is tradability in a crisis rather than distrust of any custodian, and this briefing records the stated reason rather than the inferred one. It is nonetheless the first sovereign reserve reallocation logged in this file that names geopolitical risk as its cause.**

**Bangladesh is the clearest casualty of the month.** LNG imports fell approximately **83% between July and August** — from **0.63 million tonnes** to **0.11 million tonnes** — amid the Hormuz disruption. **ZCA analysis** projects **up to $2.8 billion** in additional fossil-fuel costs for 2026. Bangladesh imports **95%** of its petroleum, draws **66%** of its electricity from natural gas, and sourced nearly **two-thirds** of its 2025 LNG through the Strait. Dhaka has approved **two spot LNG cargoes** for August and September, procured **eight cargoes** from the **UK, Australia, Malaysia and Oman**, and is seeking additional **diesel from India and China**.

**The regional picture around it.** **India** imports **85-90%** of its crude; **Pakistan** relies on foreign tankers for roughly **85%** of supply. In Pakistan and Bangladesh, businesses running diesel generators are paying **40-60% more per unit of energy** than grid power.

**Europe's bill and its winter.** EU countries have absorbed nearly **€41 billion** in extra fossil-fuel costs since March — the **Netherlands €11.5bn**, **Italy €12.7bn**, **France €10.8bn**, **Spain €8.8bn**. European gas reached about **€74.5/MWh**, the highest intraday level since **January 2023**. LNG prices are up **60% in the Atlantic** and **75% in the Pacific**; diesel and petrol are up **59%** since February 28. **There is still no EU-wide rationing and the European Commission has not invoked emergency measures**, but shortages are rising in **France** and **Hungary** and **inventories going into winter are abnormally low**.

**Iraq is buying its way around the problem.** Baghdad has begun hiring tankers for Hormuz runs through the state-run **Iraqi Oil Tankers Co.**, a step approved by the cabinet, **because commercial owners will not take the risk**. **SOMO's** September programme allocates **3.017 million bpd** of Basra crude — approximately **1.995m bpd Basra Light** and **1.02m bpd Basra Heavy** — and SOMO continues to offer **Basrah Medium and Heavy for ship-to-ship collection near the Omani coast**, outside the Strait entirely. **Saudi Arabia** is meanwhile moving **1.9 million bpd** through the **Egyptian pipeline** to the Mediterranean, into a Red Sea whose war-risk area was extended **800 kilometres** up the kingdom's west coast. **Two of the three largest Gulf producers are now routing around the waterway the United States says it controls.**

**China as a Hormuz-dependent importer.** Preliminary **Kpler** figures put Chinese imports of Iranian crude at **~534,000 bpd in August** against **~823,000 bpd in July** and a **1.4m bpd** average last year, with September and October offers collapsed and **Shandong teapots** substituting **Urals** and **fuel oil**.

**And the American consumer price.** National average retail gasoline **$4.14 per gallon**, nearly a dollar higher than a year ago, with the war polling at **31% support and 63% opposition** and voters specifically unhappy about fuel. Reporting on the deployment extension puts the cost at roughly **$1,200 per American household**, against a record **$1.5 trillion** military spending request.

**Transit and insurance state.** **Six transits** against an **85/day** pre-crisis baseline (**7% of normal**); weekly transits **102** against **130+/day** pre-war; war-risk insurance at **40.0× pre-crisis**, hull rates **7.5-10% of vessel value** per transit; war-risk claims **~$2 billion** across 70+ cases; **$7-8 of every barrel** attributable to war-risk insurance per *Lloyd's List*.

**Sources:** Bloomberg via gCaptain and The Japan Times, “Japan's Mitsui OSK Sees Risk to Hormuz Shipping Through Year-End” and “Mitsui OSK sees disruption of Hormuz shipping extending beyond 2026,” September 3-4, 2026; OilPrice.com, “Hormuz Disruptions Could Drag Into Next Year, Japanese Tanker Giant Warns,” September 2026; Bloomberg via CNN, Euronews, CNBC and Al Jazeera on De Nederlandsche Bank's gold transfer, September 2-3, 2026; The Business Standard, “Bangladesh faces up to $2.8b higher fossil fuel bill for 2026: ZCA Analysis,” September 2026; Outlook India, “Bangladesh's Energy Shock: Why India Matters In South Asia's Fuel Trade”; ORF Middle East, “Asia's Energy Stress: Regional Impact of Hormuz Crisis”; Euronews, “EU countries face nearly €41bn in extra fossil fuel costs as Hormuz crisis exposes energy vulnerability,” August 26, 2026; Trading Economics EU natural gas series, September 2026; Bloomberg, “Iraq Is in Process of Seeking Oil Tankers for Hormuz Strait Runs,” September 4, 2026; Voice of Emirates and Egypt Oil & Gas on SOMO's tenders, August-September 2026; Kpler via The China-Global South Project and Hydrocarbon Processing, August-September 2026; straits.live board, 04 September 2026 2301Z; CBS News live updates, September 3, 2026.

### September 4 Update — The Blockade's Cost Is Priced in a Number That Travels: $7-8 of Every Barrel Is War-Risk Insurance Alone (September 3, 2026)

**The decomposition.** **David Osler**, law and marine insurance editor at *Lloyd's List*: **“Roughly $7 or $8 on the price of a barrel of crude is now down to war-risk insurance alone.”** Brent trades at **$95.87** against a pre-crisis baseline near **$72** — a premium of roughly **$24**. **On Osler's figure, about a third of the war premium in the oil price is an insurance artefact rather than a physical shortage: the barrel is expensive substantially because it is dangerous to move, not only because there is less of it.** War-risk insurance premiums for high-risk transits have risen to **as much as 10% of a ship's value**, against a fraction of a percentage point in normal conditions; a VLCC valued near **$140 million** therefore faces millions of dollars of insurance cost per journey, and the straits.live board carries **$10.0 million per VLCC transit** at **40.0×** pre-crisis rates.

**The claims.** Around **$2 billion** in war-risk claims since the fighting began, across **more than 70 cases**, against **more than 72 attacks on ships since March** — the **second-largest hit to marine underwriters in more than a decade**, exceeded only by the **2024 collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge** in Baltimore. Market-wide claims for the war, terror and political violence segment are projected at **$2-3 billion** against an estimated **annual global premium volume for that entire segment of $1.5-2 billion**. **The line has consumed more than a year of its own worldwide income on one conflict.**

**The risk has spread beyond the Gulf.** Underwriters extended the war-risk area **800 kilometres further up Saudi Arabia's west coast** into the Red Sea, with the **Houthis targeting the Port of Yanbu** and Saudi-linked tankers — and **Yanbu is the Mediterranean end of the workaround**, with Saudi Arabia now moving **1.9 million barrels a day** through the Egyptian pipeline instead of through Hormuz.

**South Korea moves from exposure to deployment.** Seoul is preparing to send military assets to the Strait to support freedom of navigation, aiming to dispatch **before year-end** — the **Cheonghae Unit's 4,400-tonne destroyer *Wang Geon***, about **260 personnel** with a **naval special warfare boarding team** and **Lynx helicopters**, currently limited to Somali waters and requiring **National Assembly approval** to go further. **South Korea and Japan are the world's most Hormuz-dependent major economies**, and the Korean-operated **Senegal Prosperity** was struck off Khasab on August 31.

**India is squeezed from the Iranian side of the ledger.** Iran's **Persian Gulf Strait Authority** has blacklisted **11 more vessels**, taking the list to **56**, with **fines, detention or confiscation** threatened and any vessel cooperating with a listed ship liable to be added. **At least three Indian refiners and one global energy major** have decided to stop using listed vessels. India imports about **85% of its crude**, of which roughly **55-65%** has historically transited Hormuz; its Petroleum Ministry said in **March** that about **70%** of imports were by then arriving from outside the Strait. **The blacklist attacks the remaining fraction not by interdiction but by making the hulls uninsurable and uncharterable.**

**The Philippines pays in people.** Since **February 28**, **31 vessels carrying 421 Filipino seafarers** have been attacked in Hormuz-related incidents: **406 unharmed, 10 injured and recovered, 3 killed** — two of them this week aboard the **Sidr** — and **1 still missing**.

**Bangladesh and Pakistan remain the most structurally exposed and the least able to absorb it.** The two, with India, imported almost **two-thirds of their LNG** through Hormuz in 2025; both have minimal storage, and Bangladesh was already running a gas deficit of more than **1,300 million cubic feet per day** before the war. IEA member countries import about **29%** of the crude passing the Strait.

**And the alternative corridor acquired a great-power suitor.** President **Xi Jinping** used his Cairo state visit to urge Middle Eastern states to **oppose external interference** and to offer **Chinese cooperation on protecting shipping routes** — an offer made at the **Suez** end of the bypass that the Hormuz blockade created.

**The throughput dispute is unresolved and widened again.** Administration figures: **Vance** — **15 million barrels** overnight; **Energy Secretary Chris Wright** — **more than 17 million** on August 31; **Bessent** — flows **“nearing prewar levels”**; **US officials via CNN** — **40 escorted vessels carrying 18 million barrels**, most running dark. Tracker figures: **Kpler** — **five ships** crossing on Monday; **TankerTrackers.com** — about **4.9 million barrels a day** since mid-July; **IMF and Oxford Economics** — **fewer than five tanker crossings a day**; **straits.live** — **six transits** against an **85/day** baseline. **Goldman Sachs** (August 28) and **ISW** (September 3), the two parties with no stake in American performance, both land in the middle: **roughly two-thirds of pre-war Gulf export volume** and **~40 transits**. **51 of 244 screened tankers went AIS-dark in 24 hours, which explains the spread mechanically without resolving it, because neither side publishes a counting rule.**

### September 3 Update — The Administration Claimed a War-High 17 Million Barrels and the Ship-Trackers Put It at 9.14 Million, Then Watched It Fall to 4.63 Million in Two Days; and the War's Newest Dead Are Two Filipino Seafarers (September 2, 2026)

**The claim.** US Energy Secretary **Chris Wright** told CNBC that **more than 17 million barrels of oil transited the Strait of Hormuz by ship on Monday August 31** — a record since the war began — and that when the Saudi and Emirati bypass pipelines are included, regional exports on Monday **exceeded pre-war levels**. Approximately **20 million bpd** of crude and products passed through the Strait before February 28.

**The rebuttal is specific and methodological.** **TankerTrackers.com** co-founder **Samir Madani** called the figure **“mathemagics,”** saying Wright appeared to be **aggregating ship-to-ship transfers occurring over multiple days into a single day's count**. TankerTrackers' own figures: approximately **9.14 million barrels** exited the Arabian Sea on August 31 including Hormuz and the UAE bypass route; a **seven-day average of 8.27 million**; a **twenty-eight-day average of 6.85 million**; against a **pre-war baseline of roughly 15 million barrels through Hormuz alone**, or 20 million including petroleum products.

**And the trend since is the part the claim cannot survive.** Madani records volumes **falling to an estimated 6.81 million barrels on September 1 and 4.63 million on September 2** as hostilities resumed. **The administration selected the single best day in six months, counted it generously, and announced it as the state of the waterway on the eve of a 50% two-day collapse.** **Kpler** separately assesses Middle Eastern exports at approximately **65-70% of pre-war levels** by late August.

**The board agrees with the trackers.** straits.live at **02 September 2026 2305Z**: **6 transits** on its most recent completed day against a typical **85 per day** — **7% of the pre-crisis baseline**; **111** vessels actively transiting; **469 hulls** holding position away from berth; **74 tankers went AIS-dark in twenty-four hours**; **2,399** vessels flagged high-risk and **148** moderate-risk. **Status: closed to commercial shipping by war-risk insurance declaration.**

**Prices.** **Brent $95.32**, up **0.06%** on the day and **32.4%** above the ~$72 pre-crisis baseline. **AAA national average $4.1203/gal** against under **$3.00** before the war — roughly **37% in six months**; the board projects **$4.78/gal** if the Strait is fully closed. **War-risk insurance at 40.0× pre-crisis rates**, approximately **$10 million per VLCC transit**. **Crisis Pressure Index 92/100 (Extreme).** Reopening probability by **December 31 fell from 28% to 26%**; by **July 1, 2027 rose from 53% to 55%**.

**And the human cost landed where it has landed all war.** The two people killed in the Khasab attacks were **Filipino seafarers** aboard the **Sidr** — a **Saudi-flagged hull**, operated by Saudi Arabia's **Bahri**, carrying **Saudi crude**. **The Philippines is not a belligerent. Saudi Arabia is not a belligerent.** The **Senegal Prosperity** is operated by **South Korea's Sinokor** and Liberian-flagged. **Every party to that incident except the attacker is a neutral, and Filipino crews are the labour force of the world tanker fleet.**

**The Asian exposure is unchanged and structural.** **Qatar and the UAE supply 99% of Pakistan's LNG imports, 72% of Bangladesh's and 53% of India's.** **South Korea** holds approximately **3.5 million tonnes** of LNG and **Japan** approximately **4.4 million tonnes** in reserve — roughly **two to four weeks** of stable demand. **Japan** carries the highest disruption-risk score of any major economy at **6.4**, ahead of **South Korea at 5.3** and **India at 4.9**.

**And the financial campaign widened.** Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent**, at the G20 finance ministers' meetings: **“We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime,”** with **weekly new secondary sanctions** beginning with **Iranian banks** and extending to **airline leasing companies** and anyone doing business with the **IRGC**. **Several G20 members raised concerns about market disruption.**
