### September 2 Update — The Hulls That Were Struck Belonged to the Countries With the Least Agency in the War, and Brent Moved 4.99% in a Session (September 1, 2026)

**The price.** The **straits.live** board carried **Brent at $95.29** at its **01 September 2026 2301Z** timestamp, **+4.99%** over twenty-four hours and **+32.3%** above the ~**$72** pre-crisis baseline, with **WTI at $90.68**; **TradingEconomics** carried **$95.27, +4.60%**. This is the **largest single-session move since the twenty-nine-night pause broke** — larger than the Larak session and the "Punishment of the Aggressor" session combined. The **AAA national average** reached **$4.0954 per gallon** against under **$3.00** before the war began in February.

**The reopening curve moved the right way to be credible.** Near-dated probabilities barely changed — **September 15 at 1%**, **September 30 at 3%**, **December 31 at 28%** — while the **long-dated probability fell sharply: reopening by July 1, 2027 now 53%, down from 62%** a day earlier. **Markets did not price a short crisis getting worse; they priced a long one getting longer.**

**The victims are third parties.** Both supertankers struck off **Khasab** were carrying **Saudi crude** out of **Juaymah**: the **Sidr** run by Saudi Arabia's **Bahri**, the **Senegal Prosperity** operated by **South Korea's Sinokor**. **Neither Saudi Arabia nor South Korea is a belligerent.** This is the structural fact of the Hormuz campaign — the states absorbing its costs are overwhelmingly not the states fighting it.

**The Asian exposure ledger, itemised.** **South Korea** draws approximately **70% of its crude** and **18% of its LNG** through the Strait. **Japan** takes **over 90%** of its crude from the Middle East, with roughly **75% transiting Hormuz**. **India** takes about **40% of its oil** through the Strait and about **30% of its LNG** from Qatar and the UAE. Comparative supply-disruption risk scoring puts **Japan highest at 6.4**, **South Korea 5.3**, **India 4.9**.

**The freight and industrial channel.** **LNG carrier rates around $300,000 per day**, a roughly **650% increase**. Crude tanker rates at historic highs. Rerouting via the **Cape of Good Hope** adds **50-80%** to freight costs. War-risk premia stand at **40x pre-crisis** on the straits.live measure — roughly **$10 million** to insure a VLCC transit — against published market ranges of **3-10% of hull value** versus **0.25%** before the war, with peak-tension quotes near **$21 million** for a 270,000-dwt tanker. **Korean petrochemicals are the first heavy-industrial casualty:** **Lotte Chemical**, **LG Chem** and **Hanwha Solutions** have issued potential force-majeure notices, and **Yeochun NCC**, Korea's largest ethylene producer, has declared supply disruption. **India** is absorbing inflationary pressure on food and essential goods through logistics costs.

**The shipping picture.** **472 vessels** holding position away from berth; **151** actively transiting (26 tankers, 49 cargo, 75 other, 1 military); **114 of 325 screened tankers went AIS-dark** in twenty-four hours — **the same behaviour both stricken supertankers exhibited before they were hit**. **338** vessels flagged high-risk and **221** moderate-risk. Crisis pressure index **92**; escalation forecast index **52**, up three.

**And the policy claim that sits against all of it.** Treasury Secretary **Bessent** told the **G20 in Asheville** that the Strait of Hormuz will be a **"worthless piece of water"** within **two years**, bypassed by overland pipelines. **The same reporting notes that the Saudi, Emirati, Iraqi and Turkish pipeline agreements would take multiple years to build**, and that the Strait will remain central to the oil trade meanwhile. **Two years is longer than the market's own 53% reopening horizon and longer than any Asian importer's inventory cover.** This briefing records the claim as a **dated, falsifiable prediction with a September 2028 horizon**.

**Iran's own consumers.** Petrol queues in Tehran have run **from midnight**; officials have signalled **quota reductions** and higher prices above allotment while **denying a shortage**; presidential chief of staff **Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei** said quotas would be *"cut"* with the subsidised price unchanged; **Pezeshkian** has asked the public and the government's own vehicle fleet to exercise restraint. **The oil-exporting belligerent is rationing fuel.**

### August 25 Update — The Crisis Has Run Long Enough to Separate Policy Effects from Exposure Effects, and the Separation Is Stark (August 2026)

**Exposure did not determine outcome.** Roughly a **fifth of the world's oil** and **19% of LNG** moved through the Strait before February 28, some **80% of the oil bound for Asia**. **Japan** sources **90% of its oil from the Middle East** and is among the most exposed economies on earth. **India** is also among the most Hormuz-exposed large importers. Yet India **avoided formal fuel rationing altogether** and saw retail fuel prices rise by only about **7%** across the crisis period against a **global average of 25-30%**, while **South Korea, Bangladesh, Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, Sri Lanka and Pakistan** all moved to **standing rationing regimes**.

**What India did instead.** It absorbed the shock through the budget: an **excise-duty cut of roughly ₹10 per litre** on petrol and diesel, **forgoing about ₹1.7 lakh crore in revenue**, layered on a decade of sourcing diversification. The non-price measures were behavioural rather than restrictive — encouraging **work-from-home** and **restricting foreign travel**.

**What South Korea did.** **Licence-plate rationing** restricting vehicle use to **alternate days**, plus **temporary fuel price caps** to blunt the immediate cost pass-through. Seoul is also the **only affected state responding to the crisis with concrete plans to expand renewable generation** — a structural answer to a chokepoint problem, and the only one of its kind in the dataset.

**The rest of the Asian measure set.** **Public-transport promotion** in Bangladesh, **shorter working weeks** in Sri Lanka, **restricted business hours** in Pakistan, and **limits on cooling temperatures** in Malaysia. School closures and work-from-home mandates were used across the region in the acute March phase.

**Shipping has re-routed structurally rather than waited.** **Eight of nine major container carriers** are routing via the **Cape of Good Hope**. Market odds of a Strait reopening by **August 31** stand **under 1%** and by **December 31** at **34%** — a market saying the disruption is now a fixture to be engineered around rather than an interruption to be waited out. **Qatar's** LNG position remains impaired, with roughly **17% of export capacity lost**, about **$20bn of annual revenue foregone**, and an IMF April-vintage projection of **-14.7% for 2026**; **South Korea and Japan** continue to face critical LNG deficits from Qatari and Emirati supply.

### August 24 Update — The Bypass Acquires a Ministerial Task Force, and Iran Threatens It (August 21-24, 2026)

**The adaptation has passed from emergency measure to institutional design, which is what a chokepoint closure looks like when it stops being treated as temporary.** **France and Saudi Arabia have established a joint task force focused on energy and logistics connections between the Middle East and Europe**, meeting at **ministerial level on August 24**, alongside the **Macron-MBS summit** whose principal file is Hormuz substitution: **increased trade through Omani ports outside the Persian Gulf**, **expanded and potentially doubled pipeline capacity** in Saudi Arabia and other states, and **new regional rail links**. A standing bilateral body with a ministerial cadence is a different thing from a chartered vessel or a rerouted cargo — it is a commitment of capital on the assumption that the Strait will not be reliable for years.

**Iran has responded by putting the alternatives on its target list.** **Mohsen Rezaei** said on **August 23** that Iran would **target the oil-shipping routes out of the Persian Gulf that serve as alternatives to the Strait** if regional states join the economic war, and warned via IRNA that Tehran would not allow **"a single drop of oil"** to leave the Gulf if pressure escalates. The bypass is being **built and threatened in the same week**.

**The demand side has settled into managed scarcity.** Asian energy prices since March have run roughly **50-100% above February 2026 levels**. **South Korea and Japan** face critical **LNG deficits** from UAE and Qatari supply; South Korea has run **licence-plate rationing** and has sent a **first trial container ship through the Arctic route**; **Bangladesh, Thailand and Vietnam** ration energy; **Indonesia** caps purchases at **50 litres** and **Sri Lanka** at **15**, with Sri Lanka also on a **shortened working week**; **Pakistan** restricts business hours; **India** has imposed **work-from-home and travel restrictions**. **India is the notable outlier on price:** it **avoided formal fuel rationing altogether** and retail fuel prices have risen by only about **7%** over the crisis period against a **global average of 25-30%** — policy and sourcing diversification changing the outcome for one of the most Hormuz-exposed large importers.

**The American consumer is paying on a lag, and the freight side is paying more.** The **AAA national average** for regular gasoline stood at **$4.0986 on August 23**, ninety cents above a year earlier. **Diesel reached $5.6074**, a **record August level**, **$1.92 above the year-earlier $3.6893** and **40 cents above a month ago** — a steeper and more persistent climb than gasoline, and the one that transmits into goods prices rather than into household sentiment.

**And the crisis is changing generation policy, not only procurement.** CSIS records that the Hormuz energy crisis has generated a **tailwind for nuclear energy across Northeast Asia** — the clearest sign yet that the importing economies are treating the chokepoint's unreliability as a **structural planning assumption** rather than a transient shock. Six EU states have urged a **windfall tax** on oil companies profiting from the crisis. War-risk cover in the Strait remains at approximately **$10.0m per VLCC passage, forty times pre-crisis**, with **six P&I clubs** having withdrawn coverage.

### August 23 Update — The Bypass Is Now Being Built, Which Is What Permanence Looks Like (August 21-24, 2026)

**The important change is no longer the depth of the shortage but that capital is being spent on routes which assume the Strait stays shut.** **South Korea has sent its first trial container ship through the Arctic route** to avoid the Middle East entirely — a voyage that only makes commercial sense if the operator expects the disruption to outlast a season. On **Monday August 24** Saudi Arabia's crown prince and the French president convene the **Franco-Saudi Strategic Partnership Council** in Paris with an agenda devoted to **diversifying transport routes for energy and logistics**, including alternative maritime routes, **pipeline projects and regional rail links** between the Middle East and Europe. And **Iran itself** is floating **expanded Omani port trade, new pipelines and new rail links to bypass Hormuz** — meaning the state currently holding the chokepoint closed is investing in reducing the value of the asset it is holding. Three parties with opposed interests are building the same workaround.

**Demand-side measures have hardened from emergency response into standing policy.** **South Korea** is operating **licence-plate vehicle rationing**, restricting use to alternate days. **Bangladesh, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam** have imposed **energy rationing**. **Indonesia** caps fuel purchases at **50 litres a day** and **Sri Lanka** at **15**, with Sri Lanka also running **shorter working weeks**. **Pakistan** has restricted business hours, **Malaysia** is encouraging limits on cooling temperatures, **Bangladesh** is promoting public transport, and **India** is encouraging **work from home** and **restricting foreign travel**. India — which imports nearly **90% of its crude** and about **half its natural gas**, and is the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer — is additionally managing an **LPG supply crisis** caused directly by the disruption. **Japan and South Korea** continue drawing on **joint emergency stockpiles**.

**The price signal is elevated and politically live.** **Brent** traded near **$94** on **August 22** for a second consecutive weekly gain of roughly 6%, and the **AAA national average** US pump price stood at **$4.1024**, close to a dollar above the year-earlier level. **Six EU member states** have urged a **windfall tax on oil companies** profiting from the crisis. Beyond Asia, the **World Bank** projects **Lebanon's economy will contract 6.4%** with inflation reaching **17.5%**.

**And the traffic did not recover.** **UKMTO** recorded **21 inbound and 18 outbound** transits in the week ending **August 7** — about **4% of pre-conflict levels** — and still assesses the risk to mariners as **severe**. PortWatch's most recent published day, **August 16**, logged **one transit** against a **73-per-day** pre-crisis baseline. straits.live counted **331 hulls** holding position away from berth at **2256Z on August 22** and prices war-risk cover at **40 times pre-crisis levels**, roughly **$10 million** for a single VLCC passage, with the market-implied probability of a reopening by **September 1 below 1%**.

### August 22 Update — Rationing Becomes the Normal Condition From Seoul to Dhaka (August 2026)

**The disruption is now managed rather than absorbed.** With transits running between **one and thirteen vessels a day against a 73-a-day pre-crisis baseline**, the responses across importing states have hardened from emergency measures into standing policy.

**Northeast Asia.** **Japan** imports more than **95%** of its Middle Eastern crude through the waterway and **South Korea** more than **70%** of its total imported crude; South Korea also takes **14%** of its LNG from Qatar and the UAE against Japan's **6%**. Seoul is running **licence-plate rationing**, restricting vehicle use to alternate days. Tokyo and Seoul are **releasing oil from their joint stockpile** to moderate prices that have run above **$100 a barrel** at points in the crisis.

**South Asia is worse, because it is LNG rather than oil.** Qatar and the UAE account for **99% of Pakistan's LNG imports, 72% of Bangladesh's and 53% of India's**. **Pakistan** has moved from an LNG surplus to **record spot purchases** within a year and is running an **emergency gas management plan** that prioritises domestic and residential supply while **suspending roughly 78 million cubic feet a day to the fertiliser sector**. **Bangladesh** was scheduled to receive **115 LNG cargoes in 2026** and expects to lose about **forty**; **four of its five state-run urea fertiliser plants** have shut for at least **fifteen days**, and gas to the power sector has been cut from **870 to 820 million cubic feet a day**, with officials warning of increased load-shedding and possible blackouts. **India** is absorbing inflationary pressure on food and essential goods as energy-linked logistics costs rise.

**Southeast Asia is capping consumption directly.** **Indonesia** has limited fuel purchases to **50 litres a day** and **Sri Lanka** to **15 litres a day**.

**The financial transmission is separate from the physical one.** With the Persian Gulf designated a **"Listed Area"** by global insurers, maritime premiums across the region have surged **300-400%**, raising freight costs directly — for Bangladesh, on the ready-made garment exports that carry its economy. War-risk cover for a Hormuz transit is running near **10% of hull value**. A coalition spanning **South Korea, Japan, India, China, Vietnam, Thailand and more than thirty other states** has organised around the shortages. **None of these states is a party to the war, and none has a mechanism to end it.**

### August 1 Update — LNG Traffic Resumes After a Fortnight and Transits Hit a Two-Week High, While the Import End Stays Exposed (July 29-31, 2026)

**The first genuine easing in two weeks, and its limits.** S&P Global recorded **28 vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz on July 29**, the highest since **July 14**, driven by **resumed LNG tanker traffic after a two-week gap** along with several dark transits. **Iran-linked vessels fell to 60% of movements**, down from a 68% average in the second half of July — a composition shift that matters as much as the count, since it indicates non-Iranian operators returning to the waterway. **Bab el-Mandeb crossings rose to 39**, and very large crude carriers increasingly gathered at Egypt's **Sidi Kerir** terminal, complicating voyage logistics for cargoes routed around the Gulf.

**Throughput has not recovered.** The straits.live board on July 31 still assessed commercial transit at **11% of pre-crisis norms** — latest recorded daily volume of 10 vessels against a typical 88 per day — with **1,364 vessels stranded or anchored** in the zone, **85 AIS-dark tankers** against a 42.4 seven-day baseline, **war-risk insurance for supertankers at 8.0x peacetime rates**, and prediction markets pricing a **1% probability** of normalised traffic by August 1. Iran's Fars agency said the Revolutionary Guards **stopped two tankers** while **four others altered course**.

**The import end remains a demonstrated target.** The **July 29 drone attack** on the US-owned FSRU *Energos Winter* and the LNG carrier *Gaslog Salem* at Egypt's **Damietta** established that receiving terminals — not only export chokepoints and production facilities — are exposed. Attribution moved further from resolution on July 31: **Iran denied involvement** and alleged an Israeli false flag, while **Egypt publicly rejected** reporting that Cairo blames Iran, with drone debris under forensic analysis and no party claiming responsibility. For the importing economies the practical consequence is unchanged whatever the attribution: the risk premium now attaches to both ends of the chain.

**The dependence baseline, unchanged.** Qatar and the UAE account for **99% of Pakistan's LNG imports**, **72% of Bangladesh's** and **53% of India's**. **South Korea** holds roughly **3.5 million tonnes** and **Japan** roughly **4.4 million tonnes** of LNG in reserve — on the order of two to four weeks of stable demand. Japan relies on the Strait for close to three-quarters of its oil imports and South Korea for roughly 60% of its crude. India continues to face inflationary pressure on food and essential goods as energy-related logistics costs rise, with **Petronet LNG** and **GAIL** rationing gas to industrial customers.

### July 31 Update — The Damietta Strike Redraws the Risk Map: the IMPORT End Is Now a Target Too (July 29-30, 2026)

For five months the energy dimension of this war has been fought at a single point — the Strait of Hormuz — and the exposure of the importing economies has been measured as dependence on transit through it. That measurement is now incomplete. On **July 29, 2026** an **unclaimed drone** struck the US-owned FSRU ***Energos Winter*** at **Egypt's Damietta**, spreading fire to the LNG carrier ***Gaslog Salem*** and disrupting operations at one of Egypt's principal **gas import terminals**. It is the **first attack of this war on receiving rather than exporting infrastructure**, and the first on Egyptian soil. Attribution is unresolved: Egypt's Cabinet confirmed a drone caused it and named no perpetrator; Trump blamed Iran without presenting evidence; no party claimed responsibility.

**The transit-dependence baseline, unchanged.** Japan relies on the Strait for close to **three-quarters of its oil imports**; South Korea for roughly **60% of its crude**; India for about **half its crude imports and 60% of its natural gas**. **Qatar and the UAE together account for 99% of Pakistan's LNG imports and 72% of Bangladesh's** — and with limited storage capacity and little procurement flexibility, **Pakistan and Bangladesh remain the most acutely exposed economies in the world to this blockade**. South Asia faces the sharpest LNG deficits; South Korea and Japan face critical shortfalls in UAE and Qatari supply; India is absorbing inflationary pressure on food and essential goods as energy-linked logistics costs rise.

**Why Damietta matters to that list.** Every economy above depends not only on cargoes leaving the Gulf but on the terminals, regasification units and floating storage that receive them. Those assets are fixed, lightly defended, commercially owned and — as of July 29 — demonstrably reachable by a single one-way drone, on a coastline 2,000 km from the Strait. No comparable attack has yet occurred at an Asian or European receiving terminal, and none is forecast here. The point of record is narrower: the threat surface of the blockade is no longer bounded by the chokepoint.

**Chokepoint status.** IMF PortWatch's most recent independent count remains **10 commercial transits on July 23 against an 88-per-day pre-crisis baseline** — about 11% of normal throughput. War-risk insurance stands at **8.0× pre-crisis levels**, roughly **$2.5m to insure a single VLCC for the passage**. The straits.live tracker's July 30 vessel readings broke comparability with the prior cycle and are recorded with a flag rather than treated as a change in conditions. At the second chokepoint, **Bab el-Mandeb transits fell to 11 cargo vessels in a day** after Houthi attacks on Saudi Red Sea shipping, the lowest in months, with the July 20 Houthi maritime embargo of Saudi Arabia still in force; roughly **8% of the world's seaborne oil** passes through it.
*Sources: CNBC, "The Strait of Hormuz is facing a blockade.
